title: Let P={x∣4≤x≤10 and is even}, then is equivalent to
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Sets, Representation of Sets and Hierarchy of numbers
text: Let P = {x | 4 ≤ x ≤ 10 and x is even}. Then P is equivalent to:
solution:
A set given in set-builder form, {x : conditions on x}, is defined by testing each candidate value of x against every stated condition; only values satisfying all the conditions jointly belong to the set. When two conditions are joined by 'and', a value must pass both to qualify.

  1. The two conditions on x are: 4 ≤ x ≤ 10 (x lies in the closed interval from 4 to 10) and x is even.

  2. List every integer that satisfies the interval condition alone: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.

  3. From this list, retain only the integers that also satisfy the even condition: 4, 6, 8, 10.

  4. Collect the surviving values in roster (list) notation to obtain P.

  • Endpoint check: since the inequality uses ≤ (inclusive), both endpoints 4 and 10 qualify under the interval condition, and both are even, so both remain in P.

  • Exclusion check: 5 lies inside the interval but is odd, so the even condition removes it; 12 is even but lies outside the interval, so the interval condition removes it — both correctly stay out of P.

Therefore, P = {4, 6, 8, 10}.

title: Which of the following set is uncountable
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Finite, Infinite, Countable, and Uncountable Sets
text: Which of the following sets is uncountable?
solution:
Concept. A set is countable if its elements can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers, i.e. arranged in a single list (finite sets are also countable). A set is uncountable if no such listing exists — it is strictly “larger” than the natural numbers. The standard example of an uncountable set is the set of real numbers, proved uncountable by Cantor’s diagonal argument.

Applying this to each offered set:

  • Natural numbers can be listed directly as 1, 2, 3, 4, …, which is itself a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers, so this set is countable.

  • All integers can be listed as 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, 3, −3, …, alternating signs so every integer eventually appears at a fixed position, so this set is countable.

  • Positive rationals p/q can be placed in an infinite grid (numerator × denominator) and traversed along successive diagonals, skipping repeated values; this produces a single list of all of them, so this set is countable.

Conclusion. All three named sets are countable, so the option asserting that none of the listed sets is uncountable is the one that holds. By contrast, the real numbers — had they been offered — would be the uncountable choice, since Cantor’s diagonal argument shows the reals in [0, 1] cannot be exhausted by any list.

optionFeedback.html: The natural numbers can be written out as the single list 1, 2, 3, 4, …, which is a one-to-one correspondence with the counting numbers; a set that can be listed this way is countable, not uncountable.
The integers can be written out as 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, 3, −3, …, so every integer eventually appears at a fixed place in the list; a set that can be listed this way is countable, not uncountable.

The positive rationals p/q can be arranged in an infinite grid and traversed along diagonals (skipping duplicate values), which lists them all; a set that can be listed this way is countable, not uncountable.

All three named sets — the natural numbers, the integers, and the positive rationals — can each be arranged in a single list (a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers), so each of them is countable. None of the named sets is an uncountable set; an uncountable set such as the real numbers is not present among the named sets.

title: Which of the following is/are true: The set of real
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Finite, Infinite, Countable, and Uncountable Sets
text:
Which of the following is/are true:
S1. The set of real numbers is countable
S2. The set of rational numbers is countable
S3. The set of integers is uncountable
S4. The set of real numbers between 0 to ¼ is uncountable
solution:
Definitions: Countable means a set can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. Uncountable means it is not countable.

  • The set of real numbers is countable: False. The real numbers are uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument shows no complete listing of real numbers is possible).

  • The set of rational numbers is countable: True. Rationals can be enumerated by arranging fractions as pairs of integers (numerator, denominator), ordering those pairs (for example by increasing sum of absolute values) and skipping duplicates, giving a sequence that lists every rational number.

  • The set of integers is uncountable: False. The integers are countable; for example list them as 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, ... which gives a bijection with the natural numbers.

  • The set of real numbers between 0 and 1/4 is uncountable: True. Any nontrivial interval of real numbers has the same cardinality as (0,1). A simple bijection x ↦ 4x maps (0,1/4) to (0,1), and (0,1) is uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument.

Conclusion: The true statements are the countability of the rational numbers and the uncountability of the real numbers between 0 and 1/4. Therefore, the correct combination is: the statement that the rationals are countable and the statement that the real numbers between 0 and 1/4 are uncountable.

The rational numbers are countable because you can list them by arranging pairs of integers (numerator, denominator) and skipping duplicates. The real numbers are uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument shows there is no listing that contains every real number).

This choice is correct. The rational numbers are countable since they can be put in a sequence (for example by enumerating pairs of integers and removing duplicates). Any nontrivial interval of real numbers (such as the real numbers between 0 and 1/4) is uncountable; a bijection (scaling by 4) shows this interval has the same cardinality as (0,1), which is uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument.

This choice is incorrect because the statement that the set of real numbers is countable is false, while the statement that the real numbers between 0 and 1/4 are uncountable is true. The interval from 0 to 1/4 is uncountable for the same reason as any interval of real numbers: it can be put into a bijection with (0,1) and Cantor's diagonal argument shows (0,1) is uncountable.

This choice is incorrect because the statement that the set of integers is uncountable is false. The integers are countable: you can list them in a sequence like 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, ... which establishes a bijection with the natural numbers. The statements that the rationals are countable and that real numbers between 0 and 1/4 are uncountable are both true, but the incorrect claim about integers makes this choice wrong.

title: Which of the following sets has no proper subset?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Null, Universal, Subsets, Proper Subsets
text: Which of the following sets has no proper subset?
solution:
Correct answer: The empty set { }

Definition of proper subset: A proper subset of a set S is a subset that is strictly smaller than S (that is, a subset that is not equal to S).

  • Because the empty set has no elements, the only subset it can have is itself.

  • A proper subset must be different from the set, so there is no subset distinct from the empty set. Therefore, the empty set has no proper subsets.

title: The number of elements in the power set of is
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Power Set and its Cardinality
text: The number of elements in the power set of {{1, 2}, {2, 1, 1}, {2, 1, 1, 2}} is:
solution:
Concept

A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects. Two consequences follow directly from this definition: the order in which elements are written is irrelevant, and repeated elements are counted only once. So {a, a, b} and {b, a} denote the same set. Consequently, when one set contains other sets as its members, two member-sets that are equal collapse into a single element of the outer set.

For any set S with n distinct elements, its power set P(S) (the set of all subsets) has exactly 2n elements.

Application

Simplify each inner set using set equality:

  1. {1, 2} is already in simplest form: the elements 1 and 2.

  2. {2, 1, 1} has a repeated 1 and a reordering, so it equals {1, 2}.

  3. {2, 1, 1, 2} repeats both 1 and 2, so it also equals {1, 2}.

  4. All three members are the same set {1, 2}. As elements of the outer set they collapse to one, so the outer set is S = { {1, 2} }, which has n = 1 distinct element.

  5. Apply the cardinality rule: |P(S)| = 21 = 2.

Cross-check

List the power set explicitly: the only subsets of the one-element set { {1, 2} } are the empty set and the set itself, i.e. P(S) = { ∅, { {1, 2} } } — exactly 2 subsets, confirming the result.

Why 8 is wrong: 8 = 23 arises only if the three written entries are treated as three distinct elements. That ignores set equality — the three entries are literally the same set, so the outer set never has three elements. A video or note that arrives at 8 has counted the entries as written rather than as sets.

Note on the linked video for this question: if its explanation gives the answer as 8 (by treating the three written entries as three distinct elements), that explanation is incorrect for the reason shown above. Trust this written, step-by-step derivation, which follows directly from the definition of set equality and matches the exam's own answer key.

optionFeedback.html: The value 3 is simply the number of entries written inside the outer braces. That is a raw tally of what is on the page, not a count of subsets, so it answers a different question than the one asked.

The value 8 = 23 comes from treating the three written entries as three different members of the outer set. They are taken exactly as printed, which is the very assumption this question puts to the test.

The value 4 = 22 comes from applying set equality to only some of the three written entries rather than to all of them, so the outer collection is treated as having two distinct members. Whether two entries denote the same set is a single definite test that must be applied uniformly across every entry — not invoked for one pair and skipped for another — and this partial application is the flaw, not the formula 2n itself.

Once the three inner sets are recognised as the single set {1,2}, the outer collection holds exactly one distinct member, and a one-member set has 2 subsets — the empty set and the set itself. The value 2 reflects that single-member outer set.

title: If and are sets and union intersection then
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Set Operations – Union, Intersection, Set Difference, Symmetric Difference, and Complement
text: If A and B are sets and A union B = A intersection B, then
solution:
Solution: If A ∪ B = A ∩ B then A = B. Proof:

  1. Take any element x in A. Since A ⊆ A ∪ B and A ∪ B = A ∩ B, we have x in A ∩ B, so x is in B. Hence A ⊆ B.

  2. Similarly, take any element x in B. From B ⊆ A ∪ B and A ∪ B = A ∩ B we get x in A ∩ B, so x is in A. Hence B ⊆ A.

Since A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A, we conclude A = B. (The special case A = B = empty set also satisfies the equality, but the general conclusion remains that the two sets are equal.)

optionFeedback.html: The statement "A = empty set" is not necessarily true. The equality of union and intersection forces the two sets to be equal, but they need not be empty. For example, if A = empty set and B = {1}, then A ∪ B = {1} while A ∩ B = empty set, so the equality fails. The correct conclusion from A ∪ B = A ∩ B is that A = B.

The statement "B = empty set" is not necessarily true. The condition A ∪ B = A ∩ B does not force either set individually to be empty; it forces the two sets to be equal. For instance, with A = {1} and B = empty set the union and intersection differ, so the equality is not satisfied. The correct conclusion is A = B.

Correct. If A ∪ B = A ∩ B then every element of A is in A ∩ B, so every element of A is in B (A ⊆ B). By the same argument every element of B is in A (B ⊆ A). Therefore A = B. (Note: this also covers the empty-set case since A = B = empty set satisfies the equality.)

The choice "None of these" is incorrect. The equality A ∪ B = A ∩ B implies that every element of A lies in B and every element of B lies in A, so A and B must be equal. Therefore one of the listed options, namely "A = B", is correct.

For any two sets A and B, the set difference A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B} keeps exactly the elements of A that are absent from B. If that result still equals the whole of A, no element of A has been removed — which is possible only when no element of A is present in B at all.   1. Write the given condition: A − B = A.

  2. Apply the definition of set difference, A − B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ B}. Setting this equal to A means every element x ∈ A must satisfy x ∉ B — so no element of A lies in B.

  4. By the definition of intersection, two disjoint sets share no common elements, so A ∩ B = ∅.

  • A ∩ B = A would require A ⊆ B, i.e. every element of A also lying in B — the exact opposite of what A − B = A gives. The two can agree only in the degenerate case A = ∅, so A is not the value of the intersection in general.

Explanation and final conclusion:

Compare the sizes of the power sets by comparing the sizes of the underlying sets: if two sets S and T have power sets of the same size, then |S| = |T| because |P(S)| = 2^{|S|}.

Apply this to the problem: the equality of power sets means

  • |(A × B) ∪ (B × A)| = |A × B|.

Therefore the power sets are equal precisely in the cases: A = B, or A = ∅, or B = ∅.

Consequently, the given equality fails exactly when none of those conditions hold, i.e. when A ≠ B and both A and B are nonempty.

text: If A ={1,2}, Then no of relation possible on A which are not function?
solution:
Explanation: For the set A = {1, 2}, compute the counts step by step.

  • Number of elements in A is 2, so the Cartesian product A × A has 2 × 2 = 4 ordered pairs.

  • A relation on A is any subset of A × A, so the total number of relations is 2^4 = 16.

  • A function from A to A assigns to each of the 2 elements exactly one image in A, so the number of functions is 2^2 = 4.

  • Therefore the number of relations that are not functions is 16 − 4 = 12.

title: Consider binary relation on is defined as follows: (a,b)R(c,d) iff
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Symmetric Anti-Symmetric Asymmetric Relation and Properties
text:
Consider a binary relation R on Z ✖ Z is defined as follows:   
(a,b)R(c,d) iff a>c and b<d
then which of the following is/are true:
solution:
Relation R on Z x Z is defined by (a,b)R(c,d) iff a > c and b < d.

  • Irreflexive: No pair (a,b) can satisfy (a,b)R(a,b) because that would require a>a and b<b, which is impossible. Hence the relation is irreflexive.

  • Asymmetric: If (a,b)R(c,d) then a>c and b<d. For (c,d)R(a,b) we would need c>a and d<b, which contradicts a>c and b<d. Thus both directions cannot hold, so the relation is asymmetric.

  • Antisymmetric: Antisymmetry requires that if two elements are mutually related then they are equal. Since no distinct pairs can be mutually related (and no element is related to itself), the condition is vacuously satisfied, so the relation is antisymmetric.

  • Transitive (so "Not transitive" is false): If (a,b)R(c,d) and (c,d)R(e,f), then a>c>e implies a>e, and b<d<f implies b<f; therefore (a,b)R(e,f). Hence the relation is transitive.

Conclusion: The relation is irreflexive, asymmetric, and antisymmetric (the latter vacuously). It is also transitive, so the claim that it is not transitive is incorrect.

Asymmetric is correct. If (a,b)R(c,d) then a>c and b<d. For (c,d)R(a,b) to also hold would require c>a and d<b, which contradicts a>c and b<d. Thus both directions cannot hold simultaneously, so the relation is asymmetric.

Antisymmetric is also true (vacuously). Antisymmetry requires that if two elements relate to each other then they are equal. Here there are no distinct pairs that are mutually related (and no element is related to itself), so the condition is satisfied vacuously.

solution:
Answer: 59049 = 3¹⁰

Reasoning:
A reflexive relation must include all 5 diagonal pairs (a, a), so these pairs are fixed.

For each unordered pair of distinct elements {a, b}, antisymmetry does not allow both (a, b) and (b, a) to be present together. For each such pair, there are exactly three choices: include neither ordered pair, include (a, b) only, or include (b, a) only.

The number of unordered pairs of distinct elements is n(n - 1)/2 = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10. Therefore, the number of reflexive and antisymmetric relations is 3¹⁰ = 59049.

title: The number of Asymmetric relations of set with elements
subject: Discrete Mathematics

text: The number of Asymmetric relations of a set with 4 elements ____
solution:
Correct solution: The number of asymmetric relations on an n-element set is 3^(n(n-1)/2).

  • For each unordered pair of distinct elements {i, j} (there are n(n-1)/2 such pairs), there are three possibilities: no ordered pair between them, only (i, j), or only (j, i).

  • Diagonal pairs (i, i) cannot appear in an asymmetric relation, so there are no choices for those.

  • Multiplying the three choices for each unordered pair gives 3^(n(n-1)/2) possible asymmetric relations.

For n = 4, n(n-1)/2 = 6, so the number of asymmetric relations is 3^6 = 729.

solution:
Correct properties: Reflexive and Symmetric; not Transitive; not Irreflexive.

  • Reflexive: Every time is at distance 0 from itself, and 0 ≤ 20, so each time is related to itself.

  • Symmetric: If time x and time y differ by at most 20 minutes, then y and x differ by the same amount, so the relation holds in both directions.

  • Not Transitive: Counterexample: 10:00 and 10:20 are related (20 minutes), and 10:20 and 10:40 are related (20 minutes), but 10:00 and 10:40 are 40 minutes apart, which is more than 20, so they are not related. Thus transitivity fails.

  • Not Irreflexive: Irreflexive would require no element to relate to itself, but since every time relates to itself (difference 0 ≤ 20), the relation is not irreflexive.

title: Is relation defined over the set of integers as follows
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Transitive Relation – Definition, Count, and Properties
text: Let R be a relation on the set of integers Z, defined by aRb if and only if a is a factor of b. Then R is:
solution:
Concept

A relation R on a set is reflexive when xRx holds for every x, symmetric when xRy implies yRx, and transitive when xRy and yRz together imply xRz.

For divisibility, a divides b means that b = ak for some integer k.

Application

  1. Reflexivity: For every integer a, a = a × 1, so a divides itself. Hence aRa holds for every a.

  2. Symmetry: Symmetry need not hold. For example, 2 divides 4, but 4 does not divide 2; thus 2R4 does not imply 4R2.

  3. Transitivity: If a divides b and b divides c, write b = am and c = bn for integers m and n. Then c = a(mn), and mn is an integer, so a divides c.

Cross-check

For instance, 3 divides 6 and 6 divides 18, and indeed 3 divides 18; reversing 3 divides 6 gives 6 divides 3, which is false. Therefore R is reflexive and transitive, but not symmetric.

title: Consider relation between vertices in an undirected graph two vertices
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Equivalence Relation, Equivalence Classes, Partitions of a Set
text:
Consider a relation R on the vertices of an undirected graph: two vertices v and w are connected if and only if there is a path between them.

solution:
Answer: The connectedness relation in an undirected graph is symmetric and transitive (and also reflexive), so asymmetric and irreflexive do not hold.

  • Symmetric: If there is a path from v to w, the same sequence of edges can be traversed in reverse to produce a path from w to v (edges are bidirectional). Thus the relation is symmetric.

  • Transitive: If there is a path from v to w and a path from w to u, concatenating those paths yields a path from v to u (repeating vertices is allowed when only existence matters). Therefore the relation is transitive.

  • Asymmetric: Asymmetry would require that whenever v is related to w, w is not related to v. This contradicts the symmetry just explained, so the relation is not asymmetric.

  • Irreflexive: Irreflexive means no vertex is related to itself. But every vertex has a trivial path of length zero to itself, so each vertex is related to itself. Hence the relation is not irreflexive; it is reflexive.

title: Let {x,y,z} and let {(x,x) (y,y), (z,z),(x,y)(y,x), (y,z) be relation
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Equivalence Relation, Equivalence Classes, Partitions of a Set
text: Let P = {x, y, z} and let R = {(x, x), (y, y), (z, z), (x, y), (y, x), (y, z)} be a relation on P. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Select all that apply.)
solution:
Concept

On a set, a relation R is reflexive if (a, a) ∈ R for every element a; symmetric if (a, b) ∈ R forces (b, a) ∈ R; and transitive if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R force (a, c) ∈ R. R is an equivalence relation only when it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive together. A single missing required pair is enough to break the corresponding property.

Application to this relation

Test each property of R = {(x, x), (y, y), (z, z), (x, y), (y, x), (y, z)} on P = {x, y, z}:

  1. Reflexive: (x, x), (y, y) and (z, z) are all present, so every element relates to itself. R is reflexive.

  2. Symmetric: (x, y) and (y, x) pair up, but (y, z) is present while its mirror (z, y) is missing. R is not symmetric.

  3. Transitive: (x, y) and (y, z) are present, yet the forced pair (x, z) is absent. R is not transitive.

  4. Equivalence: an equivalence relation needs all three properties; since R fails symmetry and transitivity, R is not an equivalence relation.

Selecting the incorrect statements

The question asks which statements are incorrect (false). Judging each by its content:

  • “R is not a reflexive relation” — false, because R is reflexive.

  • “R is not a symmetric relation” — true, because R indeed fails symmetry; this statement is correct, so it is not an answer.

  • “R is a transitive relation” — false, because R is not transitive.

  • “R is an equivalence relation” — false, because R is neither symmetric nor transitive.

Result: the three false (incorrect) statements are “R is not reflexive”, “R is a transitive relation” and “R is an equivalence relation”.

optionFeedback.html: R contains (x, x), (y, y) and (z, z), so every element of P relates to itself; that is exactly what reflexivity requires. Overlooking these three self-pairs is the misstep behind doubting reflexivity.
(x, y) and (y, x) pair up, but (y, z) sits in R with no matching (z, y); a single unmatched pair is enough to break symmetry. Expecting (z, y) to exist is the trap to watch for here.
Transitivity would force (x, z) to be present, since (x, y) and (y, z) are both in R, yet (x, z) is missing. Assuming the listed pairs already close under transitivity is the error.

An equivalence relation must satisfy reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity together; R has the missing pairs (z, y) and (x, z), so two of those three requirements break down. Treating reflexivity alone as enough is the misconception.

title: Let be the real line. Consider the following subsets of
subject: Discrete Mathematics

text:
Let R be the real line. Consider the following subsets of the plane R×R:

S={(x,y) ∣ y=x+1 and 0<x<2},

T={(x,y) ∣ x−y is an integer}

Which of the following are true?

options.html: Neither S nor T is an equivalence relation on R
Both S and T are an equivalence relations on R
S is equivalence relation on R but T is not
T is equivalence relation on R but S is not

solution:
Answer: T is an equivalence relation on R but S is not.

  • S: S = {(x,y) | y = x+1 and 0 < x < 2}. S is not an equivalence relation. It is not reflexive because for any real number a the pair (a,a) would require a = a+1, which is impossible, so no (a,a) lies in S. S is not symmetric: if (x,y) is in S then y = x+1, but (y,x) would require x = y+1 = x+2, impossible. S is not transitive: if (x,y) and (y,z) are in S then z = x+2, so (x,z) does not satisfy z = x+1 and hence is not in S.

  • T: T = {(x,y) | x−y is an integer}. T is an equivalence relation because it satisfies the three properties:

    1. Reflexive: for every x, x−x = 0, and 0 is an integer, so (x,x) ∈ T.

    2. Symmetric: if x−y is an integer, then y−x = −(x−y) is also an integer, so (y,x) ∈ T.

    3. Transitive: if x−y and y−z are integers, their sum x−z is an integer, so (x,z) ∈ T.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The relation defined by x−y being an integer is an equivalence relation (it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive). The set S is not an equivalence relation: for any real a, (a,a) cannot be in S because it would require a = a+1, so S is not reflexive; S also fails symmetry and transitivity.

Incorrect. T (pairs with x−y an integer) is an equivalence relation: x−x = 0 ∈ Z (reflexive), if x−y ∈ Z then y−x = −(x−y) ∈ Z (symmetric), and sums of integers give transitivity. S is not an equivalence relation because no (a,a) lies in S (would require a = a+1), and S also fails symmetry and transitivity.

Incorrect. S is not an equivalence relation: it contains pairs with y = x+1 (and 0<x<2), so it never contains any pair (a,a) and thus is not reflexive; it also fails symmetry and transitivity. T is an equivalence relation for the reasons above (reflexive, symmetric, transitive).

Correct. The relation T = {(x,y) | x−y is an integer} is an equivalence relation because it is reflexive (x−x = 0 ∈ Z), symmetric (if x−y ∈ Z then y−x = −(x−y) ∈ Z), and transitive (sum of integers is an integer). The set S = {(x,y) | y = x+1 and 0<x<2} is not an equivalence relation: it never contains any pair (a,a) (so not reflexive) and it fails symmetry and transitivity as well.

title: Let be fixed positive integer. Let be relation defined on

text: Let n be a fixed positive integer. Let R be a relation defined on the set of integers as (a,b)∈R iff a-b is divisible by n. The relation R is
solution:
Solution: Prove each property directly.

  1. Reflexive: For any integer a, a - a = 0, and 0 is divisible by n. So (a,a) is in the relation for every a.

  2. Symmetric: If a - b is divisible by n, then b - a = -(a - b) is also divisible by n. Hence whenever (a,b) is in the relation, (b,a) is also in the relation.

  3. Transitive: If a - b = n·k1 and b - c = n·k2 for some integers k1,k2, then a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) = n·(k1 + k2), which is divisible by n. Thus whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are in the relation, (a,c) is also in the relation.

Therefore the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.

Incorrect. The relation is symmetric because if a - b is divisible by n then b - a = -(a - b) is also divisible by n. But the relation is also reflexive (a - a = 0) and transitive, so 'symmetric only' is incomplete.
Incorrect. The relation is transitive: if a - b = n·k1 and b - c = n·k2 then a - c = n·(k1 + k2). However, the relation is also reflexive and symmetric, so it is not 'transitive only'.

Correct. Short proof: Reflexive: a - a = 0 which is divisible by n. Symmetric: if a - b is divisible by n then b - a = -(a - b) is also divisible by n. Transitive: if a - b = n·k1 and b - c = n·k2 then a - c = n·(k1 + k2) is divisible by n. Therefore the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, i.e., an equivalence relation.

title: Consider natural numbers and xRy iff divides x-y. Then which
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Equivalence Relation, Equivalence Classes, Partitions of a Set
text: Consider natural numbers x and y, xRy iff 11 divides x-y. Then which of the following is false?
solution:
Solution: Show that the relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

  • Reflexive: For any natural number x, x - x = 0 and 11 divides 0, so xRx holds for every x.

  • Symmetric: If 11 divides x - y, then 11 divides y - x because y - x = -(x - y), and divisibility by 11 is unaffected by changing sign.

  • Transitive: If 11 divides x - y and 11 divides y - z, then x - z = (x - y) + (y - z) is a sum of multiples of 11, so it is a multiple of 11; hence xRz.

Conclusion: All three properties hold, so the statement that none of these is false is correct; none of the given properties is false.

optionFeedback.html: Reflexive means every natural number x must satisfy xRx. Here x - x = 0 and 11 divides 0, so the relation is reflexive.
Symmetric means if the relation holds from x to y then it holds from y to x. If 11 divides x - y, then 11 also divides y - x because y - x = -(x - y), and divisibility is unaffected by sign.

Transitive means that if xRy and yRz, then xRz. If 11 divides x - y and 11 divides y - z, then adding gives x - z = (x - y) + (y - z), which is a sum of multiples of 11, hence a multiple of 11. Thus the relation is transitive.

This statement asserts that none of the previous statements is false, i.e., all three properties are true. Since reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity all hold for this relation, this choice is correct.

text: For a set having 14 distinct elements, the number of symmetric as well as reflexive relations will be _____________.
solution:
Key idea: For a relation to be both reflexive and symmetric on a set with 14 elements, all diagonal pairs must be included and each unordered distinct pair either appears as both ordered pairs or not at all.

  • Count diagonal (reflexive) pairs: all 14 pairs (a,a) are fixed, so no choice here.

  • Count unordered distinct pairs: number is C(14,2) = 14*13/2 = 91.

  • For each unordered pair {a,b} there are 2 choices: include both (a,b) and (b,a), or exclude both. So there are 2^{91} possibilities coming from these pairs.

text: Suppose a set has 8 elements. The number of elements in the smallest equivalence relation in this set is _______.
solution:
Answer: 8.

Reasoning:

  • The relation that contains exactly those 8 pairs (the identity or equality relation) is reflexive, symmetric (trivially, since each pair is of the form (a,a)), and transitive (trivially), so it is an equivalence relation.

title: Suppose both have equivalence relations. The relation R1∩R2 is:
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Equivalence Relation, Equivalence Classes, Partitions of a Set
text: Suppose R1 & R2 both have equivalence relations. The relation R1 ∩ R2 is:
solution:
Key idea: The intersection of relations inherits properties that both relations share. If both relations are equivalence relations, their intersection will be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

  • Reflexive: For any element x, (x,x) belongs to both relations because each is reflexive, so (x,x) is in the intersection.

  • Symmetric: If (x,y) is in the intersection, then (x,y) is in both relations; since both relations are symmetric, (y,x) is in both relations and therefore in the intersection.

  • Transitive: If (x,y) and (y,z) are in the intersection, then they are in both relations; because both relations are transitive, (x,z) is in both and hence in the intersection.

Conclusion: The intersection is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation. Therefore the correct answer is: an equivalence relation.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The reflexive closure of a relation is formed by adding missing (x,x) pairs to make a relation reflexive. The intersection of two equivalence relations is not obtained by adding pairs; it consists only of pairs that belong to both relations. In fact, the intersection of two equivalence relations is already reflexive (and also symmetric and transitive), so it is not a reflexive closure.

Incorrect. A partial equivalence relation usually means a relation that is symmetric and transitive but not necessarily reflexive on the whole set. When R1 and R2 are equivalence relations on the same set, their intersection is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is a full equivalence relation rather than merely a partial equivalence relation.

Correct. If R1 and R2 are equivalence relations on the same set, then for every element x the pair (x,x) lies in both R1 and R2 (reflexivity), so (x,x) lies in the intersection. Similarly, symmetry and transitivity hold in the intersection because any relevant pair belonging to both relations has its symmetric or transitive consequences in both relations. Thus the intersection is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, i.e., an equivalence relation.

Incorrect. The intersection of two equivalence relations is an equivalence relation. It inherits reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity from both relations, so it cannot be 'not an equivalence relation' when R1 and R2 are equivalence relations on the same set.

Consider the given relations R1 and R2 on the power set of P(A) of set A as:

solution:
Correct classification and concise reasoning:

  • R1 (a ∩ b ≠ ∅): This relation is symmetric, not reflexive on the whole power set, and not transitive.

    Reasons:

    • Reflexive? No — counterexample: the empty set. ∅ ∩ ∅ = ∅, so (∅,∅) is not in the relation.

    • Symmetric? Yes — intersection is symmetric: if a ∩ b ≠ ∅ then b ∩ a ≠ ∅.

    • Transitive? No — counterexample: a = {1}, b = {1,2}, c = {2,3}. Here a ∩ b ≠ ∅ and b ∩ c ≠ ∅, but a ∩ c = ∅.

  • R2 (a ∪ b = a, equivalently b ⊆ a): This relation is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric, but not symmetric. Therefore it is a partial order on P(A).

title: Consider the following relation on the set of positive integers

text:
Consider the following relation R on the set of positive integers Z:

R = {(a, b) ∈ Z x Z | a ≡ r (mod 7) and b ≡ r (mod 7)} i.e., aRb iff a and b yield the same remainder r when divided by 7. Then R is

text: A subset of a poset is called an antichain, if every two elements of this subset are incomparable. How many antichains are there in the poset with the following Hasse diagram?
solution:
Correct count: There are 9 antichains.

Explanation:

  • Among the four elements b, c, d, e the forbidden (comparable) pairs are b with d, b with e, and c with d. The allowed incomparable pairs are (b, c), (c, e), and (d, e).

  • No three-element antichain exists because any triple from {b, c, d, e} contains at least one forbidden pair.

  • Counting antichains: the empty set (1), the five singletons {a}, {b}, {c}, {d}, {e} (5), and the three two-element antichains {b, c}, {c, e}, {d, e} (3). Total = 1 + 5 + 3 = 9.

title: The hasse diagram of lattice is shown below. Which of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Lattice – Definition, Formation, and Examples of Join and Meet Operations
text: The hasse diagram of a lattice L = {x, a, b, c, d, e, y} is shown below. Which of the following subsets of ‘L’ are sub-lattices of L?
solution:
Definition: A subset S of a lattice L is a sublattice if for every pair of elements in S, their least upper bound (join) and greatest lower bound (meet) computed in the whole lattice L also lie in S. Equivalently, S must be closed under joins and meets (as computed in L).

  • {x, a, c, y}: This is a sublattice. For every pair of elements in this set the join and meet in L remain in the set. For example, the meet and join of a and c in L are x and y respectively, both contained in the set; similar checks hold for other pairs, so the set is closed under joins and meets.

  • {x, d, c, y}: This is not a sublattice. Counterexample: the greatest lower bound (meet) of d and c in the full lattice L is a, which is not in this subset. Because the subset fails to contain that meet, it is not closed under meets and therefore not a sublattice.

  • {x, a, e, y}: This is a sublattice. Key checks such as the meet and join of a and e in L give x and y respectively (both in the subset). All other pairs similarly have their joins and meets inside the subset, so it is closed under the lattice operations.

  • {x, a, b, y}: This is not a sublattice. Counterexample: the least upper bound (join) of a and b in the full lattice L is c, which is not in this subset. Inside the subset the least upper bound of a and b would be y, differing from the join in L. Since the join in L is not contained in the subset, the subset is not closed under joins and thus not a sublattice.

Conclusion: The subsets that are sublattices are {x, a, c, y} and {x, a, e, y}.

optionFeedback.html: {x, a, c, y} is a sublattice. A subset is a sublattice if it is closed under joins (least upper bounds) and meets (greatest lower bounds) computed in the whole lattice. For this subset, for every pair of elements the join and meet taken in the full lattice L lie inside the subset. For example, the meet and join of a and c in L are x and y respectively, both of which are in the subset; similar checks hold for the other pairs. Hence the subset is closed under joins and meets.

{x, d, c, y} is not a sublattice. Find a counterexample: the greatest lower bound (meet) of d and c in the whole lattice L is a, but a is not in this subset. Because the subset does not contain the meet of two of its elements (when computed in L), it is not closed under meets and therefore is not a sublattice.

{x, a, e, y} is a sublattice. Check closure under joins and meets: for key pairs such as a and e, the meet in L is x and the join in L is y, both of which lie in the subset. Other pairs similarly have their joins and meets inside the subset. Thus the subset is closed under the lattice operations and is a sublattice.

{x, a, b, y} is not a sublattice. Provide a counterexample: the least upper bound (join) of a and b in the whole lattice L is c, but c is not in this subset. Inside the subset the least upper bound of a and b would be y, which differs from the join in L. Because the join computed in L is not contained in the subset, it is not closed under joins and therefore not a sublattice.

title: The function is mapped from natural numbers to integer numbers
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Definition of a Function – Domain, Co-domain, Range, and Count of Possible Functions
text: The function f is mapped from natural numbers to integer numbers and f(x) = x2 - 3x + 3 then what is the function f?
solution:
Given f: N → Z defined by f(x) = x^2 - 3x + 3.

Show not injective:

  • Compute f(1) = 1^2 - 3·1 + 3 = 1 and f(2) = 2^2 - 3·2 + 3 = 1.

  • Two distinct inputs (1 and 2) give the same output, so the function is not injective.

Show not surjective:

  • Check whether 0 is in the image: solve x^2 - 3x + 3 = 0.

  • The discriminant is Δ = (-3)^2 - 4·1·3 = 9 - 12 = -3, which is negative, so there are no real solutions and hence no natural solutions for f(x) = 0.

  • Therefore 0 is not in the image of f, so f is not surjective onto Z.

Conclusion:

  • Since f is neither injective nor surjective, it is not bijective.

  • Therefore the correct choice is that none of the listed properties (injective, surjective, bijective) hold.

optionFeedback.html: This function is not injective because two different natural numbers give the same output: f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 1. An injective function must map distinct inputs to distinct outputs, so this property fails.

This function is not surjective onto the integers because some integers have no preimage. For example, there is no natural number x with f(x) = 0: the quadratic equation x^2 - 3x + 3 = 0 has discriminant -3, which is negative, so it has no real (and hence no natural) solutions.

The function is not bijective because it is neither injective nor surjective. It fails injectivity (f(1) = f(2) = 1) and fails surjectivity (for example, 0 has no preimage), so it cannot be bijective.

Correct. The function is neither injective nor surjective: f(1) = f(2) = 1 demonstrates it is not injective, and the equation f(x) = 0 has no natural solutions because the discriminant is -3, so it is not surjective onto the integers. Therefore none of the listed properties hold.

title: Let be finite set having elements and let be finite
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Definition of a Function – Domain, Co-domain, Range, and Count of Possible Functions
text: Let A be a finite set having x elements and let B be a finite set having y elements. What is the number of distinct functions mapping B into A.
solution: To find the number of distinct functions mapping set B into set A, recall that a function assigns each element in the domain to exactly one element in the codomain. Here, set B is the domain with y elements and set A is the codomain with x elements. For each of the y elements in B, there are x possible choices in A to map to. Multiplying these independent choices gives x multiplied by itself y times, which equals x raised to the power of y. Thus, the number of distinct functions is x^y.

optionFeedback.html: Each element in set B has x choices in A. With y elements, this results in x raised to the power of y.
Functions between sets use exponentiation based on domain and codomain sizes, not addition or multiplication.
This represents y^x, which counts functions from A to B. For functions mapping B into A, the size of A (x) is the base and y is the exponent.
This formula calculates permutations. Functions do not require distinct outputs for each input, whereas this formula assumes no repetition.

title: What is function in terms of relation?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Definition of a Function – Domain, Co-domain, Range, and Count of Possible Functions
text: What is a function in terms of a relation?

options.html: A relation where every element of the domain is related to exactly one element of the codomain
A relation where some elements of the domain are related to more than one element of the codomain
A relation where every element of the domain is related to at least one element of the codomain
A relation where some elements of the domain are not related to any element of the codomain

solution:
Definition: In terms of relations, a function is a special type of relation that assigns to every element of the domain exactly one element of the codomain.

  • Key requirement: each input (domain element) has one and only one output (codomain element).

  • Not a function if any input has zero outputs or more than one output.

  • Example of a function: the relation { (1,2), (2,3), (3,2) } where each domain element 1, 2, 3 maps to exactly one value.

  • Non-function examples: { (1,2), (1,3) } (input 1 maps to two outputs) and domain {1,2} with relation { (1,2) } (input 2 has no output).

Therefore, the correct definition is a relation where every domain element is related to exactly one codomain element.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. A function assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the codomain: every input has a single, well-defined output.
Incorrect. If some domain elements are related to more than one codomain element, the relation fails the requirement of a function because an input would have multiple outputs.

Incorrect. Requiring each domain element to be related to at least one codomain element allows the possibility of multiple outputs for a single input. A function requires exactly one output for each input, not just one or more.
Incorrect. If some domain elements are not related to any codomain element, the relation is not a function because a function must assign an output to every element of the domain.

title: Let f:X→Y be function, and be the subsets of Which

text: Let f:X→Y be a function, A and B be the subsets of X. Which of the following conditions are true?I.If A⊆B then f(A)⊆f(B)II.fA∩fB⊆f(A∩B)
solution:
Answer: Only the first statement is true.

Proof that the first statement is true: If A ⊆ B and y ∈ f(A), then there exists x ∈ A with f(x) = y. Since A ⊆ B, that x is also in B, so y ∈ f(B). Therefore f(A) ⊆ f(B).

The second statement is false (counterexample):

  • Let X = {1, 2}, Y = {a}, and define f by f(1) = a, f(2) = a.

  • Take A = {1} and B = {2}. Then f(A) = {a} and f(B) = {a}, so f(A) ∩ f(B) = {a}.

  • But A ∩ B = ∅, so f(A ∩ B) = ∅. Hence f(A) ∩ f(B) is not contained in f(A ∩ B).

Related correct inclusion: In general we always have f(A ∩ B) ⊆ f(A) ∩ f(B), but the reverse inclusion need not hold.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The first statement is true: if A is a subset of B, then every element of A is also in B, so the image of A is contained in the image of B. The second statement is false (see counterexample below): the intersection of the images need not be contained in the image of the intersection.

Incorrect. While the first statement is true, the second statement is not necessarily true. For example, a function can map distinct elements of A and B to the same value, making the intersection of the images nonempty even when A and B are disjoint; hence the intersection of images need not be contained in the image of the intersection.

Incorrect. The first statement is true: if A⊆B then f(A)⊆f(B). The second statement is false in general; provide a counterexample where A and B are disjoint but their images overlap, so the intersection of images is not contained in the image of the intersection.

Incorrect. The first statement is true, so it is not the case that both are false. The second statement is false in general: distinct elements from A and B can share the same image, producing an intersection of images that does not come from the intersection of A and B.

title: Let be function from to and be function from to
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Composition of Functions – Definition, Properties, and Examples
text: Let g be a function from B to C and f be a function from A to B. Which of the following properties of function composition is incorrect?

options.html: If f and g∘f are onto, then g is also onto.
If f and g∘f are both one-to-one, then g is also one-to-one.
If f and g are both onto, then g∘f is also onto.
If f and g are both one-to-one, then g∘f is also one-to-one.

solution:
Concept

For f : A → B and g : B → C, the composition g∘f : A → C is defined by (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)). Surjectivity is tracked by following preimages backward, while injectivity is tracked by pulling an equality backward through the functions.

For injectivity, the composition tests g only on the image f(A). Thus injectivity of g on all of B follows from injectivity of g∘f only when f(A) covers B.

Application

  1. If g∘f is onto, then for every c ∈ C there is an a ∈ A with g(f(a)) = c. Setting b = f(a) gives g(b) = c, so g covers C.

  2. If both f and g are onto, choose b ∈ B with g(b) = c and then a ∈ A with f(a) = b. Hence g(f(a)) = c, so the composition covers C.

  3. If both f and g are one-to-one and g(f(x₁)) = g(f(x₂)), injectivity of g gives f(x₁) = f(x₂), and injectivity of f gives x₁ = x₂.

  4. If only f and g∘f are one-to-one, g is constrained on f(A) but not necessarily on B \ f(A). Thus g can assign the same value to two distinct elements of B when at least one lies outside f(A), without the composition detecting that collision.

Cross-check

Take A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, and C = {0}. Define f(1) = 1 and g(1) = g(2) = 0.

  • The function f is one-to-one because its domain has one element.

  • The composition g∘f maps 1 to 0 and is also one-to-one.

  • The function g is not one-to-one because g(1) = g(2) although 1 ≠ 2.

Result

Therefore, the incorrect property is: if f and g∘f are both one-to-one, then g is also one-to-one.

optionFeedback.html: Surjectivity of g∘f supplies, for each c ∈ C, an a ∈ A satisfying c = g(f(a)). The point f(a) lies in B, which is the domain on which g is evaluated.
Injectivity of g∘f constrains g on the subset f(A). The equality f(A) = B is the surjectivity condition on f, whereas injectivity of f concerns distinct inputs in A having distinct images.
Surjectivity of g supplies, for each c ∈ C, a b ∈ B satisfying g(b) = c. Surjectivity of f supplies an a ∈ A satisfying f(a) = b.
Injectivity of g converts g(f(x₁)) = g(f(x₂)) into f(x₁) = f(x₂). Injectivity of f then converts that equality into x₁ = x₂.

title: The function is mapped from natural number to integer numbers
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: One-to-One (Injective) Function – Definition, Count, and Properties
text: The function f is mapped from natural number to integer numbers and f(x) = x2 -2x + 3 . Consider N as a natural number and Z as Integer number , what is the function f : N -> Z ? 2, 4, 10, 28, 82, …
solution:
Answer: Injective (assuming the standard convention N = {1,2,...}).

Rewrite the function:

f(x) = x^2 - 2x + 3 = (x-1)^2 + 2

  • Proof of injectivity: Assume f(m) = f(n). Then (m-1)^2 = (n-1)^2, so |m-1| = |n-1|. This gives either m = n or m + n = 2. If natural numbers are taken as 1,2,..., the equation m + n = 2 forces m = n = 1, so in all cases m = n. Therefore f is one-to-one on N = {1,2,...}.

  • Failure of surjectivity: Since (x-1)^2 >= 0, we have f(x) >= 2 for every natural x (with N = {1,2,...}). Thus integers such as 0, 1 and all negative integers are not in the image of f, so f is not onto Z.

  • Edge case about the definition of N: If N is defined to include 0, then f is not injective because f(0) = 3 = f(2). Under that convention the function would fail to be injective.

Conclusion: Under the common convention N = {1,2,...}, f is injective but not surjective onto Z.

If f(m) = f(n) then (m-1)^2 = (n-1)^2, so |m-1| = |n-1|, which forces m = n (the only other possibility m + n = 2 gives m = n = 1). Thus the function is one-to-one (injective) on N = {1,2,...}. Note: if N were taken to include 0, the function would not be injective because f(0) = f(2) = 3.

Incorrect. The function always yields values at least 2 because f(x) = (x-1)^2 + 2 >= 2 for all natural x (with N = {1,2,...}). Therefore integers such as 0, 1 and all negative integers are not produced by f, so it is not surjective onto Z.
Incorrect. While the function is injective on N = {1,2,...}, it is not surjective onto Z because its values are always >= 2. So it cannot be both injective and surjective onto Z.

Incorrect. The function is injective on N = {1,2,...} (see proof), so 'none of the above' is not correct. However, it is not surjective onto Z, so the correct description is that the function is injective but not surjective.

text:

solution:
Final answer: Two functions are bijections: f(x) = 2x + 1 and f(x) = x³. The function f(x) = x² + 1 is not a bijection.

f(x) = 2x + 1 — Injective: If f(x1) = f(x2) then 2x1 + 1 = 2x2 + 1, so 2x1 = 2x2 and x1 = x2. Thus the function is one-to-one.

For surjectivity: Surjective: For any real y, choose x = (y - 1)/2 which is real. Then f(x) = 2((y-1)/2) + 1 = y, so every y has a preimage. Therefore f is a bijection.

f(x) = x² + 1 — Not injective: For example, f(1) = 1² + 1 = 2 and f(-1) = (-1)² + 1 = 2, so two different inputs give the same output. Hence it is not one-to-one.

Also note: the range of x² + 1 is [1, ∞), so values less than 1 have no preimage; therefore the function is not surjective. Combining these observations, f(x) = x² + 1 is not a bijection.

f(x) = x³ — Injective: If x1³ = x2³ then x1 = x2 (the cube function is strictly increasing), so it is one-to-one.

For surjectivity: Surjective: For any real y, x = ³√y is real and satisfies f(x) = (³√y)³ = y. Thus every real y has a preimage, so f is a bijection.

Conclusion: Exactly two of the given functions are bijections: 2x + 1 and x³.

title: The function defined by f(x) is
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Bijective Function – Definition, Count, and Properties
text: The function f: [0,3]→[1,29] defined by f(x) = 2x3 - 15x2 + 36x + 1 is
solution:
Concept: A function f: A → B is injective (one-to-one) when distinct inputs always produce distinct outputs, and is surjective (onto) when the values it produces cover the entire stated codomain B. By standard convention, interval notation like [0, 3] denotes every real number between 0 and 3 (a continuous interval), not just the integers 0, 1, 2, 3 — this convention is what allows the derivative and continuity argument below to apply.

Application: For f(x) = 2x3 − 15x2 + 36x + 1 on [0, 3]:

  1. Differentiate: f'(x) = 6x2 − 30x + 36 = 6(x − 2)(x − 3).

  2. Solve f'(x) = 0 within [0, 3]: the critical points are x = 2 and x = 3.

  3. Check the sign of f'(x): it is positive on [0, 2) (f is increasing) and negative on (2, 3) (f is decreasing) — so f rises then falls, meaning it is not monotonic on [0, 3].

  4. A non-monotonic function fails the horizontal-line test: since f increases up to x = 2 and then decreases, some output value is produced by two different inputs, so f is not injective.

  5. Evaluate f at the boundary and critical points: f(0) = 1, f(2) = 29, f(3) = 28.

  6. Because f is continuous, on [0, 2] it takes every value from 1 up to 29, and on [2, 3] it takes every value from 28 down to 29 — the union of these two ranges is exactly [1, 29].

  7. [1, 29] is precisely the stated codomain, so every element of the codomain is attained, meaning f is surjective.

Cross-check: Pick a value in the overlap, say y = 28.5. Solving 2x3 − 15x2 + 36x + 1 = 28.5 gives one root in (0, 2), where f is rising toward 29, and a second root in (2, 3), where f is falling from 29 to 28. Two distinct inputs producing the same output independently confirms non-injectivity, while the endpoint values 1 and 29 confirm the full codomain is covered.

Result: So the function is surjective but not injective.

The derivative changes sign at the interior turning point, so the function rises and then falls and repeats an output value — confirming it is not one-to-one — while the values it attains across [0, 3] span exactly the stated codomain [1, 29], confirming every codomain value is reached.

It also bases its codomain comparison only on the two endpoint values, leaving out the value at that turning point.

title: Consider the mapping and as described below: defined by f₁(x)

text:
Consider the mappings f1 and f2 defined as follows:

f1: ℝ → ℝ, where f1(x) = x2 + x for x ∈ ℝ.

f2: ℤ → ℤ, where f2(y) = 2y for y ∈ ℤ.

Here, ℝ is the set of real numbers and ℤ is the set of integers. Which statement is true?

options.html: f1 is neither injective nor surjective; f2 is injective but not surjective.
f1 is injective but not surjective; f2 is injective but not surjective.
Both f1 and f2 are injective as well as surjective.
f1 is not injective but is surjective; f2 is injective but not surjective.

solution:
Concept

A function is injective when distinct inputs never produce the same output. It is surjective onto its codomain when every codomain element has at least one preimage.

To test these properties, use a repeated-output counterexample for injectivity and characterize the range for surjectivity.

Application

  1. For f1, compare two distinct inputs: f1(0) = 0 and f1(−1) = (−1)2 + (−1) = 0. Hence f1 is not injective.

  2. Complete the square: f1(x) = x2 + x = (x + 1/2)2 − 1/4. Since a square is non-negative, the range of f1 is [−1/4, ∞), not all of ℝ. Hence f1 is not surjective onto ℝ.

  3. For f2, if f2(y1) = f2(y2), then 2y1 = 2y2, so y1 = y2. Hence f2 is injective.

  4. Every value of f2 is even. No odd integer, such as 1, equals 2y for an integer y. Hence f2 is not surjective onto ℤ.

Cross-check

The vertex of x2 + x is at x = −1/2 with minimum value −1/4, confirming the range found above; and f2(ℤ) = 2ℤ confirms that only even integers occur.

Therefore, f1 is neither injective nor surjective, whereas f2 is injective but not surjective.

optionFeedback.html: The classification follows from the values: f1 repeats an output for distinct inputs and misses real values below its minimum, while f2 maps distinct integers to distinct even outputs and omits odd integers.
The claim about f1 relies on the common mistake of treating every function as one-to-one, without checking whether distinct inputs can share an image.
Treating both mappings as bijections assumes that every displayed formula automatically covers its codomain uniquely; the classification requires separate injectivity and surjectivity tests.
The claim about f1 treats an unbounded domain as if it guaranteed full codomain coverage; domain size alone does not establish surjectivity.

title: Number of cycles of length that are possible in the
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Types of Graphs – Finite, Infinite, Null, Trivial, Complete
text: Number of cycles of length 4 that are possible in the complete bipartite graph k4,6 is ____.
solution:
Answer: 90

Explanation:

  • The complete bipartite graph splits vertices into two parts of sizes 4 and 6.

  • Any 4-cycle must use two vertices from the part with 4 vertices and two vertices from the part with 6 vertices.

  • Number of ways to choose two vertices from the first part is C(4,2) = 6, and from the second part is C(6,2) = 15.

  • Each choice of two vertices from each part yields exactly one 4-cycle (relabelings or starting points do not give distinct cycles), so multiply the counts: 6 × 15 = 90.

solution:
To find the maximum number of spanning trees (Tₙ) for a complete graph K₅, we use Cayley's formula:

Tₙ = n^(n-2)

For K₅, n = 5:

T₅ = 5^(5-2) = 5³ = 125

Thus, the maximum number of spanning trees for K₅ is 125.

text: Let G be a loop-free undirected graph with n vertices. If G has 56 edges and G^C (the complement of G) has 80 edges, then what is the value of n?
solution:
Number of edges in G plus the number of edges in G^C (the complement of G) equals n(n - 1)/2.

56 + 80 = n(n - 1)/2

136 = n(n - 1)/2

272 = n(n - 1)

n^2 - n - 272 = 0

Solve the quadratic: n = (1 + sqrt(1 + 4·272))/2 = (1 + sqrt(1089))/2 = (1 + 33)/2 = 17.

title: Let be complete bipartite graph given below. Which of the

text: Let K2,2 be a complete bipartite graph given below, with parts {1, 2} and {3, 4} and edges 1-3, 1-4, 2-3 and 2-4. Which of the following is the total number of paths of length 3 from vertex 1 to vertex 4?
solution:
Concept

In graph theory a path is a walk in which no vertex is repeated; its length is its number of edges. A walk of length k allows vertices (and edges) to repeat, and the count of walks of length k between two vertices equals the [u][v] entry of the k-th power of the adjacency matrix. So "number of paths" and "number of walks" are different quantities, and a path of length 3 must visit 4 distinct vertices.

Setup

The complete bipartite graph K2,2 has parts V1 = {1, 2} and V2 = {3, 4}, with every left vertex joined to every right vertex. Its edges are 1-3, 1-4, 2-3 and 2-4. Because edges only go between the two parts, any path must alternate sides at every step.

Application

A path of length 3 from 1 to 4 uses 4 distinct vertices in the order 1, x, y, 4. Trace the alternation:

  1. From 1 the first step must cross to the right part: the neighbours of 1 are 3 and 4. It cannot be 4 (that is the destination and would leave only 2 edges, repeating vertex 4), so the second vertex is 3.

  2. From 3 the next step crosses back to the left part: neighbours of 3 are 1 and 2. Vertex 1 is already used, so the third vertex is 2.

  3. From 2 the last step crosses to the right part to reach 4: 2-4 is an edge, completing 1 → 3 → 2 → 4.

No other choice of distinct intermediate vertices works, so exactly one simple path of length 3 exists: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4. Hence the count is 1.

Cross-check

Counting walks instead (allowing repeats) gives four: 1→3→1→4, 1→3→2→4, 1→4→1→4 and 1→4→2→4 — this is the adjacency-matrix value A3[1][4] = 4. Three of these repeat a vertex, so they are walks, not paths. Removing them leaves the single simple path, confirming the answer is 1.

optionFeedback.html: The value 1 is the number of three-edge routes from vertex 1 to vertex 4 that use four different vertices: in K2,2 each step must cross between the parts {1, 2} and {3, 4}, and the route 1 → 3 → 2 → 4 does exactly that.

The value 2 is the number of three-edge routes from vertex 1 to vertex 4 that come back to vertex 1 at the middle step: those routes are 1 → 3 → 1 → 4 and 1 → 4 → 1 → 4, each leaving vertex 1 and immediately returning to it.
The value 3 is the number of three-edge routes from vertex 1 to vertex 4 in which at least one vertex occurs twice: those routes are 1 → 3 → 1 → 4, 1 → 4 → 1 → 4 and 1 → 4 → 2 → 4.

The value 4 is the number of three-edge routes from vertex 1 to vertex 4 when a vertex may be revisited, that is the adjacency-matrix entry A3[1][4]: 1 → 3 → 1 → 4, 1 → 3 → 2 → 4, 1 → 4 → 1 → 4 and 1 → 4 → 2 → 4.

text: What is the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph having 10 vertices?
solution:
To find the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with 10 vertices, we need to consider the structure of a bipartite graph. A bipartite graph has two disjoint sets of vertices, and edges only exist between vertices of different sets.

The number of edges is maximized when the graph is complete bipartite, meaning every vertex in one set is connected to every vertex in the other set.

For 10 vertices, the maximum number of edges occurs when the two sets are as equal as possible. Splitting 10 vertices into two sets of 5 each gives the maximum number of edges.

The number of edges is then 5 × 5 = 25.

Thus, the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with 10 vertices is 25.

title: The number of distinct simple graphs with up to three
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Number of Graphs – Counting of Simple, Undirected, Unlabeled
text: The number of distinct simple graphs with up to three nodes is
solution:
Concept: By convention, when a graph-counting question does not explicitly say "labeled," "distinct simple graphs" means non-isomorphic graphs — two graphs count as the same if relabeling the vertices of one produces the other. So the count is obtained by enumerating distinct edge-arrangements (shapes) after removing relabelings that produce the same shape, not by treating each vertex-labeling as a separate graph.

Application: Count the non-isomorphic simple graphs for n = 1, 2, and 3 nodes, then sum them:

  1. n = 1 node: only 1 possible graph — a single isolated vertex (no edge is possible).

  2. n = 2 nodes: only 1 possible edge exists between the two nodes, so there are 2 non-isomorphic graphs — no edge, or one edge.

  3. n = 3 nodes: 3 possible edges exist among the three pairs. Grouping configurations that are the same shape under relabeling leaves 4 non-isomorphic graphs — 0 edges (empty), 1 edge, 2 edges (a path), and 3 edges (a triangle).

  4. Summing across all three sizes: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

Cross-check: This matches OEIS sequence A000088 (count of unlabeled simple graphs on n nodes), which gives 1, 2, 4 for n = 1, 2, 3. Contrast this with the labeled-vertex convention: with 3 distinguishable nodes there are 2³ = 8 possible labeled graphs on the 3 possible edges, giving 1 + 2 + 8 = 11 overall. However, 11 is not among the four options offered here (15, 10, 7, 9), and the standard convention for "distinct graphs" without an explicit "labeled" qualifier is to count non-isomorphic shapes. So 7 is the correct count among the given options.

text: Determine the numbers of undirected labeled simple graphs (connected and disconnected) with n vertices.
solution:
Counting all labeled simple graphs on n vertices: A simple undirected graph on n labeled vertices is completely determined by choosing, for each of the C(n,2) possible unordered vertex pairs — C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 — whether that pair is an edge or not. Since these C(n,2) choices are made independently and each pair has exactly two outcomes (edge present or edge absent), the total number of distinct labeled simple graphs on n vertices is 2C(n,2).

  1. Count the number of unordered vertex pairs: C(n,2), which equals n(n-1)/2.

  2. Each of these C(n,2) possible edges can independently be present or absent — 2 choices per pair.

  3. Multiply the 2 independent choices across all C(n,2) pairs: total graphs = 2C(n,2).

Why no separate connected-only count is needed here: Every graph on these n vertices is either connected or disconnected — the two categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so the connected graphs and the disconnected graphs together account for every possible graph. Since this question asks for the total across both categories, the count above already includes every disconnected graph and every connected graph; deriving how many of the 2C(n,2) graphs are connected is not needed to answer it.

  • n=2: C(n,2) = 1, so total graphs = 21 = 2 — the empty graph (disconnected) and the single-edge graph (connected); 1 + 1 = 2, matching the total.

  • n=3: C(n,2) = 3, so total graphs = 23 = 8 — enumerating: 1 empty graph and 3 graphs with exactly one edge are disconnected (4 total), while 3 graphs with exactly two edges (paths covering all 3 vertices) and 1 triangle with all three edges are connected (4 total); 4 + 4 = 8, matching the total.

title: Consider the following statements. There is no graph with VG=12

text:
Consider the following statements.

S1: There is no graph G with VG=12 and EG=28 in which each vertex is of degree either 3 or 4

solution:
Let p be the number of vertices of degree 3. Thus, (12-p) are of degree 4.

By the handshaking lemma, the sum of degrees is twice the number of edges: 2 × 28 = 56.

So, 3p + 4(12-p) = 56.

Simplifying: 3p + 48 - 4p = 56 → -p = 8 → p = -8.

Since p cannot be negative, no such graph exists. Thus, S1 is true.

For S2, assume p vertices have degree 3 and (12-p) have degree 6.

Sum of degrees: 3p + 6(12-p) = 56.

Simplifying: 3p + 72 - 6p = 56 → -3p = -16 → p = 16/3.

Since p is not an integer, no such graph exists. Thus, S2 is true.

Therefore the maximum possible number of vertices is 23.

title: For which of the following, Euler Circuit is never possible
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Graph Traversal – Walk, Path, Trail, Circuit, and Connected Graphs
text: For which of the following, Euler Circuit is never possible if number of vertices is greater than 2
solution:
Euler circuit condition: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.

  • Complete graph K_n: Each vertex has degree n-1. If n is odd then n-1 is even and K_n has an Euler circuit; if n is even then n-1 is odd and K_n does not. So K_n can admit an Euler circuit for some values of n.

  • Cycle graph C_n: Every vertex has degree 2 (even). For n ≥ 3 the cycle is connected, so C_n always has an Euler circuit.

  • n-dimensional cube Q_n: Each vertex has degree n. If n is even then all vertices have even degree and Q_n has an Euler circuit; if n is odd then all vertices have odd degree and Q_n does not. Thus Q_n sometimes admits an Euler circuit.

  • Wheel graph W_n: The hub (central) vertex has degree n-1 and each rim vertex has degree 3. For the standard wheel graphs with n ≥ 4 the rim vertices have degree 3 (odd), so not all vertices are even degree and an Euler circuit is impossible. Therefore wheel graphs do not admit an Euler circuit for the usual range of n (so they are the correct choice for the graph that never has an Euler circuit in the standard definitions).

Conclusion: Among the listed graphs, the wheel graph never admits an Euler circuit under the standard definition (because rim vertices have odd degree), so the wheel graph is the correct answer.

n-dimensional cube Q_n: every vertex has degree n. If n is even then all vertices have even degree and Q_n has an Euler circuit; if n is odd then all vertices have odd degree and Q_n does not. Thus Q_n sometimes has an Euler circuit (when n is even) and so is not the graph that never admits an Euler circuit.

title: Maximum number of edges in simple graph with vertices and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Graph Traversal – Walk, Path, Trail, Circuit, and Connected Graphs
text: Maximum number of edges in a simple graph with ‘n’ vertices and ‘k’ components is:
solution:
Concept: For a fixed number of vertices split between two component-sizes a and b (a + b constant), the total edge count C(a,2) + C(b,2) is maximized when a and b are as unequal as possible — because C(x,2) grows quadratically, concentrating vertices into one large component always beats spreading them out. So to maximize edges across exactly k components on n vertices, make one component as large as possible and connect it completely, while every other component is reduced to a single isolated vertex (0 edges).

  1. Let the large component have m vertices; the other k − 1 components share the remaining n − m vertices.

  2. To add zero extra edges from the other k − 1 components, each of them must be a single isolated vertex, so n − m = k − 1, giving m = n − k + 1.

  3. Make the large component a complete graph on m = n − k + 1 vertices; a complete graph on m vertices has m(m − 1)/2 edges.

  4. Substituting m = n − k + 1: edges = (n − k + 1)(n − k + 1 − 1)/2 = (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2.

Cross-check: take n = 5, k = 2. The formula gives (5 − 2)(5 − 2 + 1)/2 = 3 × 4/2 = 6. Directly: a complete graph on 4 vertices (K4) has 4×3/2 = 6 edges plus one isolated vertex, total 6 — and no other 2-component split of 5 vertices beats this (a 3+2 split gives only C(3,2) + C(2,2) = 3 + 1 = 4 edges), confirming the "as unequal as possible" principle.

So the maximum-edge count for n vertices in k components is (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2 — the expression matching this value among the options is correct.

title: Which of the following statements for simple graph is correct?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Graph Traversal – Walk, Path, Trail, Circuit, and Connected Graphs
text: Which of the following statements for a simple graph is correct?

options.html: Every trail is a path as well as every path is a trail

solution:
Concept

A walk is any sequence of vertices and edges connecting them, where both vertices and edges may repeat. A trail is a walk in which no edge repeats. A path is a walk in which no vertex repeats. In a simple graph, at most one edge joins any pair of vertices, so an edge is uniquely identified by its two endpoint vertices; reusing an edge would force at least one of those two vertices to be revisited. Consequently, a walk that never revisits a vertex can never reuse an edge either, which makes the path condition strictly stronger than the trail condition.

Application

  1. A walk satisfying the path condition has every vertex distinct.

  2. In a simple graph an edge is determined uniquely by its two endpoint vertices, so reusing an edge in the walk would require revisiting at least one endpoint vertex.

  3. Since the path condition rules out revisiting any vertex, it also rules out reusing any edge, so every path automatically satisfies the trail condition.

Cross-check

Testing the reverse direction with a triangle graph on vertices A, B, C: the closed walk A-B-C-A uses the three distinct edges AB, BC, CA, so it satisfies the trail condition, yet it revisits vertex A, so it fails the path condition. This confirms the implication holds only in the path-to-trail direction, not the reverse.

Contrast

  • "Every trail is a path": the triangle trail A-B-C-A above satisfies the trail condition while revisiting vertex A, so this direction does not hold.

  • "Every trail is a path as well as every path is a trail": this needs both directions to hold, but the trail-to-path direction fails as shown above, so the two conditions are not equivalent.

  • "Path and trail have no relation": the path condition (distinct vertices) has just been shown to force the trail condition (distinct edges), so the two are related by containment rather than being unconnected.

The vertex-distinctness of a path always forces edge-distinctness in a simple graph, so every path is a trail, while the converse fails: the correct statement is Every path is a trail.

It treats path membership as implying trail membership, that is, the path category as contained within the trail category.

title: The length of Hamiltonian Path in connected graph of vertices
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Euler and Hamiltonian Graphs – Definitions, Conditions, and Examples
text: The length of Hamiltonian Path in a connected graph of n vertices is
solution:
Concept: A Hamiltonian Path in a graph visits every vertex exactly once, without revisiting any vertex and without needing to return to its starting vertex. For any such path linking n vertices in sequence, the number of edges is n-1 — the same principle by which a spanning tree on n vertices always has exactly n-1 edges, since each edge joins one consecutive pair of vertices and a sequence of n items has exactly n-1 consecutive pairs.

Application:

  1. Represent the Hamiltonian Path as an ordered sequence of vertices v1, v2, …, vn, since it visits each of the n vertices exactly once.

  2. Each edge of the path joins one consecutive pair in this sequence: (v1,v2), (v2,v3), …, (vn-1,vn).

  3. Count the consecutive pairs in a sequence of n vertices: there are exactly n-1 such pairs.

  4. Each pair contributes exactly one edge, so the path contains exactly n-1 edges in total.

Cross-check: For n = 3 vertices joined as A-B-C, the Hamiltonian Path has edges AB and BC — 2 edges, matching n-1 = 3-1 = 2. Contrast this with a Hamiltonian Cycle on the same n vertices: a cycle adds one further edge that returns from the last vertex back to the first, closing the sequence into a loop. That extra closing edge is exactly why a Hamiltonian Cycle has n edges — one more than a Hamiltonian Path on the same n vertices.

Therefore, the length of a Hamiltonian Path in a connected graph of n vertices is n-1.

title: Graph with number of vertices greater and equal than three
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Euler and Hamiltonian Graphs – Definitions, Conditions, and Examples
text:
A graph G with number of vertices greater and equal than three i.e. (n≥3) is a Hamiltonian graph,
if the degree of each vertex is greater and equal to ....
solution:
Correct criterion: For a simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices, if every vertex has degree at least n/2, then the graph is Hamiltonian (Dirac's theorem).

Proof sketch:

  • Assume every vertex has degree ≥ n/2. Let C be a longest cycle in the graph.

  • If C contains all vertices, it is a Hamiltonian cycle and we are done. Otherwise pick a vertex x not on C.

  • Vertex x has at least n/2 neighbors on C. These neighbors divide C into many segments, so two neighbors of x on C are not consecutive along C. By connecting x into C between such nonconsecutive neighbors, one can form a longer cycle that includes x, contradicting the maximality of C.

  • This contradiction implies C must include all vertices; hence the graph is Hamiltonian.

Remarks: The condition is sufficient but not necessary. Also note the maximum possible degree in an n-vertex simple graph is n−1, so suggestions like degree equal to n or multiples of n are impossible.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A vertex cannot have degree equal to the number of vertices because a vertex is not adjacent to itself; the maximum possible degree for a vertex in an n-vertex simple graph is n−1. Requiring degree equal to n is impossible. A much weaker, sufficient condition is that every vertex has degree at least half the number of vertices (n/2).

title: Graph is non-planar if and only if it contains subgraph
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Planar Graphs – Kuratowski’s Theorems, Homorphism and examples
text: A graph is non-planar if and only if it contains a subgraph homomorphic to
solution:
Answer: A graph is non-planar if and only if it contains a subgraph homeomorphic to K3,3 or K5.

Explanation (Kuratowski's theorem):

  • Kuratowski's theorem states that a finite graph is non-planar exactly when it contains a subdivision (a homeomorphic copy) of K5 or K3,3.

  • Homeomorphic (a subdivision) means you may replace edges by paths by inserting degree-2 vertices; the resulting graph preserves the same connectivity pattern as the original.

  • K5 is the complete graph on five vertices and K3,3 is the complete bipartite graph with partitions of size three; these two are the minimal forbidden subdivisions for planarity, so every non-planar graph contains a subdivision of one of them.

  • Other graphs mentioned in the choices (for example K2,3 or K6) are not the correct characterization: K2,3 is not one of the two Kuratowski obstructions, and K6, while non-planar, is not required as a subdivision in every non-planar graph.

Therefore the correct characterization is: a graph is non-planar iff it contains a subgraph homeomorphic to K3,3 or K5.

optionFeedback.html: This choice lists K3,2 (same as K2,3) and K5. The standard characterization of non-planar graphs is not K3,2 but K3,3 together with K5. K3,2 is not one of the two Kuratowski graphs that must appear (as a subdivision) in every non-planar graph.

This choice lists K3,3 and K6. While K3,3 is one of the two forbidden graphs, K6 is not required by the characterization. The theorem states K5 and K3,3 (or their subdivisions) are the obstructions to planarity; K6 may be non-planar but it is not part of the minimal Kuratowski pair that characterizes all non-planar graphs.

This choice lists K2,3 and K5. K5 is one of the two Kuratowski graphs, but K2,3 (same as K3,2) is not the correct bipartite obstruction — the correct one is K3,3. Therefore this option is not the correct characterization of non-planar graphs.

title: Consider finite connected planar graph with vertices with all of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Euler Formula – Planar Graph Formula, Applications, and Derived Relations
text: Consider a finite connected planar graph with n vertices with all of degree 4 and 10 regions. Find the number of vertices in the graph.
solution:
Answer: 8

Step 1: Euler's formula

For any connected planar graph, n - e + r = 2, where n is the number of vertices, e the number of edges, and r the number of regions (including the outer region).

Step 2: Given

  • The graph is connected and planar.

  • All vertices have degree 4.

  • The number of regions is r = 10.

Step 3: Relate vertices and edges

By the Handshaking Lemma, the sum of degrees equals 2e. Since every vertex has degree 4, 4n = 2e, so e = 2n.

Step 4: Solve for the number of vertices

Substitute e = 2n and r = 10 into Euler's formula:

  1. n - e + r = 2

  2. n - 2n + 10 = 2

  3. -n + 10 = 2 ⇒ -n = -8 ⇒ n = 8

Step 5: Verify

  • Edges: e = 2n = 16.

  • Check Euler: 8 - 16 + 10 = 2, which is correct.

Any graph G is a set of vertices and edges i.e., G=(v,e). Which of the following graphs are planar? (MCQ)
