solution:
Planarity criterion: For any simple graph with v ≥ 3, a necessary condition for planarity is e ≤ 3v − 6. If this inequality is violated the graph is definitely non‑planar. If the inequality holds, the graph may be planar (the bound is necessary but not sufficient).

  • Complete graph on 5 vertices: v = 5, e = 10. Compute 3v − 6 = 3×5 − 6 = 9, and 10 ≤ 9 is false. Therefore this graph is non‑planar.

  • Graph with 12 vertices and 18 edges: v = 12, e = 18. Compute 3v − 6 = 3×12 − 6 = 30, and 18 ≤ 30 is true. The edge count passes the necessary bound, so this graph can be planar based on the given information.

  • Graph with 25 vertices and 56 edges: v = 25, e = 56. Compute 3v − 6 = 3×25 − 6 = 69, and 56 ≤ 69 is true. The edge count passes the necessary bound, so this graph can be planar based on the given information.

Conclusion: The two graphs with counts (12,18) and (25,56) meet the necessary inequality and therefore are the graphs that can be planar; the complete graph on 5 vertices is non‑planar.

title: Which of the following is/are correct
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Graph Coloring – Vertex Coloring, Edge Coloring, Chromatic Number, and Coloring Theorems
text: Which of the following is/are correct

options.html: Cycle graph of n vertices is ⌈n/2⌉ chromatic
Every tree with two or more vertices is 2-chromatic

solution:
Correct statements:

  • Every 2-chromatic graph is bipartite. Reason: If a graph needs only two colors, its vertices can be split into two color classes with no edges inside a class, which is exactly the definition of a bipartite graph.

  • Every tree with two or more vertices is 2-chromatic. Reason: Trees are acyclic and therefore bipartite; any tree with at least one edge requires two colors (a single-vertex tree is 1-chromatic).

Incorrect statements:

  • Cycle graph of n vertices is ⌈n/2⌉ chromatic. Reason: The chromatic number of a cycle C_n is 2 when n is even and 3 when n is odd, so the expression ⌈n/2⌉ is not the correct general formula (for example, C_3 has chromatic number 3 but ⌈3/2⌉ = 2).

  • For colouring any planar graph at maximum we need 5 colours. Reason: This is false because the four-color theorem states that four colors suffice for any planar graph, so 5 is not the least maximum required. (Historically there is a five-color theorem showing 5 colors suffice, but the tight bound is 4.)

Therefore, the correct statements are: Every 2-chromatic graph is bipartite, and every tree with two or more vertices is 2-chromatic.

title: Consider the following statements: There exists no simple, undirected and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Graph Coloring – Vertex Coloring, Edge Coloring, Chromatic Number, and Coloring Theorems
text:
Consider the following statements:

P: There exists no simple, undirected and connected graph with 80 vertices and 77 edges.

Q: All vertices of Euler graph are of even degree.

R: Every simple, undirected, connected and acyclic graph with 50 vertices has at least two vertices of degree one.

S : There exits a bipartite graph with more than ten vertices which is 2-colorable.

What is the number of correct statements among the above statements.
solution:
Answer: 4 — all four statements are correct.

  • P is true. A connected simple graph with n vertices has at least n−1 edges, so for 80 vertices it needs at least 79 edges. Having only 77 edges cannot yield a connected graph.

  • Q is true. An Eulerian graph (one that has an Euler circuit) requires every vertex to have even degree; therefore all vertices of an Euler graph are of even degree.

  • R is true. A simple, connected, acyclic graph is a tree. Any tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves (vertices of degree one), so a tree on 50 vertices has at least two degree-one vertices.

  • S is true. Bipartite graphs are exactly the graphs that can be colored with two colors (2-colorable). There exist bipartite graphs with more than ten vertices (for example, a path with 11 vertices), so the statement holds.

Therefore the number of correct statements is 4.

optionFeedback.html: The choice "1" is incorrect. All four statements P, Q, R and S are true: a connected simple graph with 80 vertices needs at least 79 edges so 77 edges cannot be connected; an Eulerian graph has all vertices of even degree; a connected acyclic graph with 50 vertices is a tree and trees with at least two vertices have at least two leaves; and bipartite graphs are 2-colorable and can easily have more than ten vertices.

The choice "2" is incorrect. Each of the four statements is true: connectivity requires at least 79 edges for 80 vertices, Eulerian graphs have all vertices of even degree, trees on 50 vertices have at least two degree-one vertices, and bipartite graphs are 2-colorable and can have more than ten vertices. Therefore the correct count is four, not two.

The choice "3" is incorrect. In fact all four statements are true: P is true because a connected simple graph on 80 vertices needs at least 79 edges; Q is true because Eulerian graphs have only even-degree vertices; R is true because a connected acyclic graph (a tree) on 50 vertices has at least two leaves; S is true because bipartite graphs are 2-colorable and can have more than ten vertices.

The choice "4" is correct. Reasoning: P is true since a connected simple graph with 80 vertices must have at least 79 edges; Q is true because an Eulerian (Euler) graph has every vertex of even degree; R is true because a connected acyclic graph with 50 vertices is a tree and every tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves (degree-one vertices); S is true because bipartite graphs are exactly the 2-colorable graphs and there exist bipartite graphs with more than ten vertices (for example, a path on 11 vertices).

solution:
Concept

The line graph L(G) turns each edge of G into a vertex, and joins two such vertices exactly when their edges share an endpoint in G. So a statement "L(G) is of type T whenever G is of type T" is FALSE the moment a single G of that type produces an L(G) outside T. One counterexample per claim settles it.

Testing each statement

  1. (P) Cycle → cycle. A cycle Cn has n edges arranged in a ring; each edge shares an endpoint only with its two neighbours, so the n edge-vertices reconnect into a ring of length n. Thus L(Cn) = Cn. TRUE.

  2. (Q) Clique → clique. In K4 the two edges {1,2} and {3,4} share no endpoint, so their edge-vertices are NOT adjacent in L(K4). Hence L(K4) is missing edges and is not complete (it is the octahedron). FALSE.

  3. (R) Planar → planar. The star K1,5 is planar, but all 5 of its edges meet at the centre, so every pair of edge-vertices is adjacent: L(K1,5) = K5, which is non-planar. A planar G produced a non-planar L(G). FALSE.

  4. (S) Tree → tree. The claw K1,3 is a tree, but its 3 edges pairwise share the centre, so L(K1,3) = K3 = C3, a triangle (a cycle, not a tree). FALSE.

Cross-check

Only (P) survives, and it survives for every n. (Q), (R) and (S) each fall to a single small graph, so exactly one statement is true.

Result

Only statement (P) is true.

optionFeedback.html: Each of (P), (Q), (R), (S) must be checked separately. The cycle claim (P) is the one that withstands every counterexample, since a cycle's edges always reconnect into a cycle of the same length.
The planar claim (R) does not hold: a star such as K1,5 is planar, yet its line graph is K5, which is non-planar, so planarity is not preserved by the line-graph operation.
This option relies solely on the planar claim (R). A star such as K1,5 already shows the planar claim breaks — its line graph K5 is non-planar — so a claim built only on (R) does not hold.

This bundles in the clique claim (Q) and the tree claim (S). K4 shows a clique's line graph is the octahedron, not complete, and the claw K1,3 has the triangle K3 as its line graph, so neither (Q) nor (S) can be included.

text: An undirected graph G (V, E) contains n (n > 2) nodes named v1 , v2 ,...,vn. Two nodes vi and vj are connected if and only if 0 <│i−j│≤2. Each edge (vi , vj ) is assigned a weight i+j. The cost of the minimum spanning tree of such a graph with 7 nodes is ______?
solution:
Answer: 43

Explanation: Construct the minimum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. For n = 7, edges exist between nodes that are one apart and two apart; each edge between vi and vj has weight i + j.

  • Edges between consecutive nodes vi and vi+1 have weights: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 (these are 2i+1 for i = 1..6).

  • Edges between nodes two apart vi and vi+2 have weights: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 (these are 2i+2 for i = 1..5).

Apply Kruskal: pick the smallest-weight edges that do not form a cycle until all 7 nodes are connected.

  1. Pick edge between v1 and v2 with weight 3.

  2. Pick edge between v1 and v3 with weight 4.

  3. Pick edge between v2 and v4 with weight 6 (connects v4).

  4. Pick edge between v3 and v5 with weight 8 (connects v5).

  5. Pick edge between v4 and v6 with weight 10 (connects v6).

  6. Pick edge between v5 and v7 with weight 12 (connects v7).

Total cost = 3 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 43.

solution:
The graph G has vertices corresponding to all permutations of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The total number of vertices is 5! = 120.

Each vertex represents a permutation, and an edge exists between two vertices if one permutation can be obtained from the other by swapping two adjacent numbers.

Step 1: Find the degree y of a vertex.

For any permutation, the number of adjacent swaps possible is equal to the number of adjacent pairs in the sequence. In a sequence of 5 elements, there are 4 adjacent pairs: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5).

Thus, each vertex has degree 4. So, y = 4.

Step 2: Find the number of connected components z.

Any permutation can be transformed into any other permutation by a sequence of adjacent swaps. This is a well-known result in permutation group theory: adjacent transpositions generate the symmetric group.

Therefore, the graph is connected, and there is only one connected component. So, z = 1.

Step 3: Find the number of edges p.

Use the handshaking lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices is equal to twice the number of edges.

Sum of degrees = number of vertices × degree of each vertex = 120 × 4 = 480.

So, 2p = 480, which gives p = 240.

Step 4: Compute y + z + p.

y + z + p = 4 + 1 + 240 = 245.

Therefore, the final answer is 245.

title: Binary operation on set of integers is defined as x⊕y=x
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Closure-Algebraic Structure, Associative-SemiGroup,  Identity-Monoid
text:
A binary operation ⊕ on the set of integers is defined as

x⊕y = x2 + y2

Which one of the following statements is TRUE about ⊕?
solution:
Concept

A binary operation ⊕ on a set S is commutative if a⊕b = b⊕a for every a, b in S. It is associative if (a⊕b)⊕c = a⊕(b⊕c) for every a, b, c in S. Commutativity and associativity are independent properties — an operation can satisfy one without the other, so each must be tested separately.

Applying it to this operation

Here the operation is x⊕y = x2 + y2, defined on the integers.

Test commutativity

  1. Compute x⊕y = x2 + y2.

  2. Compute y⊕x = y2 + x2.

  3. Ordinary addition is commutative, so x2 + y2 = y2 + x2. Hence x⊕y = y⊕x for all integers — the operation IS commutative.

Test associativity

  1. Left grouping: (x⊕y)⊕z = (x2 + y2)⊕z = (x2 + y2)2 + z2.

  2. Right grouping: x⊕(y⊕z) = x⊕(y2 + z2) = x2 + (y2 + z2)2.

  3. These two expressions are not equal in general, so the operation is NOT associative.

Cross-check with a counterexample

Take x = 1, y = 1, z = 0:

  • (1⊕1)⊕0 = (1 + 1)2 + 0 = 22 + 0 = 4.

  • 1⊕(1⊕0) = 1 + (1 + 0)2 = 1 + 12 = 2.

Since 4 ≠ 2, associativity fails. The operation is commutative but not associative.

optionFeedback.html: Reaching this choice means running two independent checks: a swap test on x⊕y vs y⊕x, and a regrouping test comparing (x⊕y)⊕z with x⊕(y⊕z), i.e. (x2 + y2)2 + z2 against x2 + (y2 + z2)2. Both tests must be carried out explicitly and the small case x = 1, y = 1, z = 0 evaluated before settling on this combination.

This is chosen by assuming the two properties always travel together, so neither is tested separately. They are independent: the regrouping test compares squaring an inner sum, (y2 + z2)2, with the inner squares it would replace — those are not interchangeable, so the associativity half cannot be asserted without actually evaluating both groupings.

This is chosen by reading the swap test as a failure, but x2 + y2 is written symmetrically in its two inputs, so the swap test cannot be the one that breaks; and the associativity half here is asserted without running the regrouping comparison, so neither half of this choice is supported by a completed test.

This is chosen by treating the swap test as a failure, yet exchanging the two inputs in x2 + y2 leaves the expression unchanged by inspection, so the swap test does not fail — selecting 'neither' discards a property the form shows directly and skips the separate regrouping test entirely.

title: Which of the following algebraic structure form group? The set
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Inverse Property and  Group
text:
Which of the following algebraic structure form a group?

A: The set of integers under Subtraction

B: The set of irrational numbers under multiplication

C: The set of real numbers under subtraction

D: The set of real number under multiplication

How many statements are true _________
solution:
The set of integers under subtraction

  • Closure: Subtraction of two integers is an integer. Satisfied.

  • Associativity: Subtraction is not associative; for example (1 − 2) − 3 = −4, whereas 1 − (2 − 3) = 2. Not satisfied.

  • Identity: 0 is a right identity because a − 0 = a, but 0 is not a two-sided identity (0 − a ≠ a in general). A group requires a two-sided identity. Not satisfied.

  • Inverse: Because associativity and a two-sided identity fail, the inverse axiom is not satisfied for a group.

  • Conclusion: This structure is not a group.

The set of irrational numbers under multiplication

  • Closure: The product of two irrational numbers need not be irrational. For example, √2 × √2 = 2, which is rational. Not satisfied.

  • Associativity: Multiplication is associative. Satisfied.

  • Identity: The multiplicative identity is 1, but 1 is not an irrational number. So the identity is not in the set. Not satisfied.

  • Inverse: Because the identity is not in the set, we cannot have the required inverses for a group. Not satisfied.

  • Conclusion: This structure is not a group.

The set of real numbers under subtraction

  • Closure: Subtraction of two real numbers is a real number. Satisfied.

  • Associativity: Subtraction is not associative, so the associativity axiom fails. Not satisfied.

  • Identity: 0 is a right identity (a − 0 = a) but not a two-sided identity (0 − a ≠ a in general). A group requires a two-sided identity. Not satisfied.

  • Inverse: Without a two-sided identity and associativity, the inverse axiom cannot hold for all elements. Not satisfied.

  • Conclusion: This structure is not a group.

The set of real numbers under multiplication

  • Closure: Product of two real numbers is real. Satisfied.

  • Associativity: Multiplication is associative. Satisfied.

  • Identity: The multiplicative identity 1 is in the set. Satisfied.

  • Inverse: Every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse, but 0 does not. Since 0 is in the set and lacks an inverse, the inverse axiom fails for the full set of real numbers.

  • Conclusion: The set of all real numbers under multiplication is not a group. (However, the set of nonzero real numbers under multiplication does form a group.)

Final answer

None of the given algebraic structures form a group. Thus, the number of true statements is: 0

title: Where a*b LCM (a,b). Then is

text: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60}. Define the operation a * b = LCM(a, b). Then (A, *) is a:
solution:
Step 1: Check for closure. The least common multiple (LCM) of any two elements in A is also an element of A. Since A contains all divisors of 60, the LCM of any two divisors of 60 is a divisor of 60; hence A is closed under the operation *.

Step 2: Associativity. LCM is associative: LCM(a, LCM(b, c)) = LCM(LCM(a, b), c). Therefore, * is associative.

Step 3: Identity element. An identity element e satisfies a * e = a for all a in A. For the LCM operation, e = 1 because LCM(a, 1) = a for all a in A. Thus, 1 is the identity element.

Step 4: Inverses. An inverse of an element a is an element b such that a * b = e = 1. The only element in A with such an inverse is 1 (since LCM(1, 1) = 1). For any a ≠ 1, there is no b in A with LCM(a, b) = 1, so other elements are not invertible.

Step 5: Conclusion. Since A is closed under *, the operation is associative, and A has an identity element 1, but not every element has an inverse, (A, *) is a monoid (a semigroup with an identity element).

title: Which of the following is/are necessarily property of Group?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Inverse Property and  Group
text: Which of the following is/are necessarily a property of Group?
solution:
Answer: Associativity; Existence of Identity; Existence of Inverse for every element (these are necessary properties). Commutativity is not necessary. Also note that closure under the operation is a required axiom but was not listed among the options.

Group axioms (all required):

  • Closure: the product of any two elements of the set is again in the set.

  • Associativity: (a·b)·c = a·(b·c) for all elements a, b, c.

  • Identity: there exists an element e such that e·a = a·e = a for every a.

  • Inverse: for each element a there exists an element a⁻¹ with a·a⁻¹ = a⁻¹·a = e.

Why commutativity is not required:

A group need not satisfy a·b = b·a for all a, b. Groups that do are called abelian; many standard groups are non-abelian.

Counterexample (non-commutative group): the permutation group on three elements (S3) under composition, or the group of invertible 2×2 real matrices under matrix multiplication. In these groups some pairs of elements do not commute.

Thus the correct choices are: Associativity; Existence of Inverse for every element; Existence of Identity.

Associativity is required: the group operation must satisfy (a·b)·c = a·(b·c) for all elements a, b, c in the group.
Every element must have an inverse: for each element a there exists an element a⁻¹ such that a·a⁻¹ = a⁻¹·a = identity.
An identity element must exist: there is an element e such that for every element a in the group, e·a = a·e = a.

Claim: G ⊕ H is abelian if and only if G and H are abelian.

Proof. First suppose G and H are abelian. For any (g1,h1),(g2,h2) in G ⊕ H we have (g1,h1)(g2,h2) = (g1g2,h1h2). Since g1g2 = g2g1 in G and h1h2 = h2h1 in H, this equals (g2g1,h2h1) = (g2,h2)(g1,h1). Hence G ⊕ H is abelian.

Conversely, suppose G ⊕ H is abelian. Let e_H denote the identity in H. For any g1,g2 in G consider (g1,e_H) and (g2,e_H) in G ⊕ H. Their product equality gives (g1g2,e_H) = (g2g1,e_H), so g1g2 = g2g1. Thus G is abelian. The same argument with identities in G shows H is abelian.

Therefore G ⊕ H is abelian precisely when both G and H are abelian.

title: Which one of the following is not necessarily property of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Commutative Property and Abelian Groups
text: Which one of the following is not necessarily a property of a group?
solution:
Correct answer: Commutativity is not necessary for a group.

A group must satisfy these properties:

  • Closure: the operation on any two elements produces another element of the set.

  • Associativity: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c) for all elements a, b, c.

  • Identity: there exists an element e such that e * a = a * e = a for every a.

  • Inverse: for each element a there exists b with a * b = b * a = identity.

Explanation:

Commutativity means a * b = b * a for all elements a and b. This property is required only for Abelian (commutative) groups, not for all groups.

Example: The symmetric group S3 (the permutations of three objects) satisfies closure, associativity, identity, and inverses, so it is a group, but it is not commutative because some permutations do not commute. Thus commutativity is not a necessary condition for being a group.

Associativity is required by the definition of a group: for all a, b, c we must have (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). Without associativity the structure is not a group. For example, subtraction on integers is not associative, so (Z, -) is not a group.

Every element must have an inverse in a group: for each a there exists b such that a * b = b * a = identity. This is a required property. For instance, integers under addition have inverses (negatives), but natural numbers under addition do not, so the naturals under + are not a group.

A group must have an identity element e such that e * a = a * e = a for every element a. This existence of an identity is a required property of a group; without an identity the structure cannot be a group.

title: Which of the following options are true if is finite
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Determining the Order of Elements within Groups
text: Which of the following options are true if G is a finite group of 54 elements?

options.html: The total number of subgroups of G will be equal to 16.
The size of the largest possible proper subgroup of G is 27.
The size of the smallest subgroup of G is 5.

solution:
By Lagrange's theorem: the order of any subgroup divides 54.

Therefore the possible orders of subgroups are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 54. Orders 1 and 54 correspond to the trivial subgroup and the whole group.

Existence of a subgroup of order 27:

  • Let n3 be the number of Sylow 3-subgroups. By Sylow's theorems, n3 divides 2 (the factor of 2 in 54) and n3 ≡ 1 (mod 3).

  • The only integer dividing 2 and congruent to 1 modulo 3 is 1, so n3 = 1.

  • Hence there is a unique (and therefore normal) Sylow 3-subgroup of order 27, so a subgroup of order 27 does exist.

Conclusion: The largest possible proper subgroup of G has order 27, so the correct statement is that the size of the largest possible proper subgroup is 27.

Brief notes on the other statements:

  • A group of order 54 is not necessarily cyclic; cyclicity would require an element of order 54, which is not guaranteed.

  • The total number of subgroups depends on the group's structure. For example, a cyclic group of order 54 has one subgroup for each divisor (8 subgroups), so '16' is not generally true.

  • The smallest subgroup has order 1 (the trivial subgroup). Order 5 is impossible because 5 does not divide 54.

Incorrect. The total number of subgroups is not determined solely by the order of the group. Different groups of order 54 can have different numbers of subgroups. For instance, a cyclic group of order 54 has one subgroup for each divisor of 54 (8 subgroups), so 16 is not a universal value.

Correct. By Lagrange's theorem possible subgroup orders include 27, and Sylow's theorems guarantee a subgroup of order 27: the number of Sylow 3-subgroups divides 2 and is congruent to 1 modulo 3, so there is exactly one Sylow 3-subgroup of order 27. Thus the largest possible proper subgroup has order 27.

solution:
A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false. To determine if a sentence is a proposition, check if it is a statement (not a question, command, or expression with variables) and has a definite truth value.

Option A: "What is your name?" is a question, not a statement, so it is not a proposition.

Option B: "x + 2 = 5" contains a variable. Its truth value depends on x, so it is not a proposition (it is a predicate).

Option C: "The sky is blue" is a declarative statement that can be evaluated as true or false, so it is a proposition.

Option D: "Walk to the store" is a command, not a statement, so it is not a proposition.

title: Which of the following are tautologies? (ii) (iii) (iv)
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Types of Logical Cases – Tautology, Contradiction, Contingency, Satisfiability, and Validity
text:
Which of the following are tautologies?

(i) (p ∧ q) → p

(ii) p → (p ∨ q)

(iii) ¬p → (p → q)

(iv) (p ∧ (p → q)) → q

(v) ¬(p → q) → p
solution:
Let's break down each statement to determine if it's a tautology (always true):

(i) (p ∧ q) → p:This is true because if p and q are both true, then p is certainly true. If p and q are not both true, the implication is still true because the antecedent is false.

(ii) p → (p ∨ q):This is always true because if p is true, then p∨q is true regardless of q. If p is false, the implication is true regardless of q (as the antecedent is false).

(iii) ¬p → (p → q):This is true because if p is false, then p→q is true regardless of q. If p is true, the implication still holds.

(iv) (p ∧ (p → q)) → q:This is always true because if p is true, p→q means q must also be true. If p is false, the implication holds automatically.

(v) ¬(p → q) → p:This is true. If p→q is false (meaning p is true and q is false), the implication forces p to be true.

title: Which of the following argument is valid?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Types of Logical Cases – Tautology, Contradiction, Contingency, Satisfiability, and Validity
text: Which of the following arguments is valid?

options.html: {p → q, r → s, r ∨ p, ¬q} ⊢ p
{p → q, r → s, r ∨ p, ¬q} ⊢ q
{p → q, r → s, r ∨ p, ¬q} ⊢ s

solution:
Concept: An argument (a set of premises together with a conclusion) is valid when the conclusion is a necessary consequence of the premises under truth-preserving rules of inference. Three such rules are used here — Modus Ponens: from P → Q and P, infer Q. Modus Tollens: from P → Q and ¬Q, infer ¬P. Disjunctive Syllogism: from P ∨ Q and ¬P, infer Q.

  1. The premises are: (1) p → q, (2) r → s, (3) r ∨ p, (4) ¬q.

  2. Apply Modus Tollens to (1) and (4): p → q with ¬q gives ¬p.

  3. Apply Disjunctive Syllogism to (3) and the derived ¬p: r ∨ p with ¬p gives r.

  4. Apply Modus Ponens to (2) and the derived r: r → s with r gives s.

Cross-check (proof by contradiction): suppose the conclusion s were false, i.e. ¬s. Then from (2) r → s and ¬s, Modus Tollens gives ¬r. From (3) r ∨ p and ¬r, Disjunctive Syllogism gives p. From (1) p → q and p, Modus Ponens gives q — but premise (4) states ¬q, a direct contradiction. So ¬s is impossible together with the premises, confirming s must hold.

Since every step above follows by a valid rule of inference and an independent contradiction check confirms it, the premises necessarily and only establish the conclusion s — that is the valid argument among those offered.

optionFeedback.html: From p → q together with ¬q, Modus Tollens yields ¬p — the opposite of this option's conclusion — so the premises do not support concluding p.
¬q is one of the given premises itself, so concluding q directly contradicts what is already stated; this argument cannot be valid.
From r ∨ p and the derived ¬p, Disjunctive Syllogism yields r — the opposite of this option's conclusion — so the premises do not support concluding ¬r.

Working through the premises step by step — using Modus Tollens, then Disjunctive Syllogism, then Modus Ponens in turn — every step is forced by the premises, and the chain terminates at s: the premises jointly and necessarily establish s, making this argument valid.

The sentence 'No students are allowed to carry book' means that for every individual, if they are a student, then they are not allowed to carry a book.

This is a universal statement, so we use the universal quantifier ∀x.

The predicate 'Student(x)' represents 'x is a student', and 'Carrybook(x)' represents 'x is allowed to carry a book'.

The statement 'if x is a student, then x is not allowed to carry a book' is written as Student(x) → ~Carrybook(x).

Combining these, the full formula is ∀x (Student(x) → ~Carrybook(x)).

title: Which of the following is/are correct for given sentence: “No
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Quantifiers – Universal and Existential
text:
Which of the following is/are correct for given sentence:

“No student is allowed to carry laptop or mobile”
solution:
Formalization: No student is allowed to carry laptop or mobile can be written as ∀x(student(x) → ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x))).

  • Equivalence to the conjunction form: apply De Morgan's law ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q to get ∀x(student(x) → ¬carry_laptop(x) ∧ ¬carry_mobile(x)).

  • Equivalence to the disjunction form: rewrite implication p → q as ¬p ∨ q to get ∀x(¬student(x) ∨ ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x))).

  • Equivalence to the negated-existence form: use the identity ∀x φ ≡ ¬∃x ¬φ and simplify inside:

    Start: ∀x(student(x) → ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x)))

    ≡ ¬∃x ¬(student(x) → ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x)))

    Inside: ¬(student → ψ) ≡ student ∧ ¬ψ, so ¬∃x(student(x) ∧ ¬¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x)))

    Double negation simplifies to give ¬∃x(student(x) ∧ (carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x))).

Conclusion: the three formulas above are equivalent and correctly express the sentence. The remaining formula ¬∃x(student(x) ∧ (carry_laptop(x) ∧ ¬carry_mobile(x))) is not equivalent because it only forbids students who carry a laptop and not a mobile, but it does not forbid a student who carries only a mobile. For example, a student carrying only a mobile would violate the original sentence but would satisfy that last formula.

Therefore the correct equivalent formalizations are the conjunction form, the negated-existence form, and the disjunction form given above.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This states that for every x, if x is a student then x does not carry a laptop and does not carry a mobile. Using De Morgan's law on the negation of a disjunction, this is equivalent to forbidding a student from carrying a laptop or a mobile.

Correct. This denies the existence of a student who carries a laptop or a mobile. By moving the universal quantifier to an existential with negation (∀x φ ≡ ¬∃x ¬φ) and simplifying, this is equivalent to the original sentence.

Incorrect. This only forbids a student who carries a laptop and does not carry a mobile. It does not forbid a student who carries only a mobile. For example, a student carrying only a mobile would violate the original sentence but would not be ruled out by this formula, so the formula is too weak.

Correct. Rewriting implication as a disjunction (p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q) gives a universal formula that says either x is not a student or x does not carry a laptop or mobile, which is equivalent to the original sentence.

title: Match the following Lists List-I List-II There are at most
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Quantifiers – Universal and Existential
text:
Match the following Lists       

                   List-I                                                                                      List-II
A. There are at most two apples.                               1. ∀x∀y∀z((Apple(x) Λ Apple(y) Λ Apple(z)) → (x =y V x=z V y = z))
B. There are exactly two apples.                                2. ∀x∀y((Apple(x) Λ Apple(y)) → (x = y V y = x))
C. There is at most one apple.                                    3. ∃x∃y(Apple(x) Λ Apple(y) Λ (x ≠ y) Λ ∀z(Apple(z) → ((z= x) V (z = y))))
D. There is exactly one apple.                                     4. ∃x(Apple(x) Λ (Apple(y) → (x = y)))

Codes:
        A    B   C   D
(a)    1     2    3   4
(b)    3     2    1   4
(c)    1     3    2   4
(d)    3     1    2   4
solution:
Let Apple(p) mean: p is an apple.

Interpretation of the formulas:

  • Formula 1: ∀x∀y∀z((Apple(x) ∧ Apple(y) ∧ Apple(z)) → (x = y ∨ x = z ∨ y = z)). This forbids three distinct apples, so there are at most two apples.

  • Formula 2: ∀x∀y((Apple(x) ∧ Apple(y)) → x = y). This forces any two apples to be identical, so there is at most one apple.

  • Formula 3: ∃x∃y(Apple(x) ∧ Apple(y) ∧ x ≠ y ∧ ∀z(Apple(z) → (z = x ∨ z = y))). This asserts there exist two distinct apples and every apple is one of them, so exactly two apples.

  • Formula 4: ∃x(Apple(x) ∧ (Apple(y) → x = y)). Read as intended with universal quantification over y: ∃x(Apple(x) ∧ ∀y(Apple(y) → x = y)). This asserts a unique apple, so exactly one apple.

Final matching and justification:

  • A (There are at most two apples) → Formula 1, because formula 1 rules out three distinct apples.

  • B (There are exactly two apples) → Formula 3, because formula 3 asserts two distinct apples and that no other apples exist.

  • C (There is at most one apple) → Formula 2, because formula 2 makes any two apples identical, allowing at most one.

  • D (There is exactly one apple) → Formula 4 (read with ∀y), because it asserts existence of an apple and that any apple must equal that one.

Therefore the correct code is: A → 1, B → 3, C → 2, D → 4 (the third choice).

optionFeedback.html: The proposed mapping is: A → 1, B → 2, C → 3, D → 4. This is incorrect. A → 1 and D → 4 are correct, but B → 2 is wrong because B states exactly two apples while formula 2 forces any two apples to be identical (so at most one apple). C → 3 is wrong because C says at most one apple but formula 3 asserts the existence of two distinct apples (exactly two).

The proposed mapping is: A → 3, B → 2, C → 1, D → 4. This is incorrect. D → 4 is correct, but A → 3 is not correct because A asks for at most two apples while formula 3 asserts exactly two (which is stronger). B → 2 is wrong because formula 2 enforces at most one apple, contradicting "exactly two." C → 1 is wrong because formula 1 allows up to two apples while C requires at most one.

The proposed mapping is: A → 1, B → 3, C → 2, D → 4. This is correct. Formula 1 rules out three distinct apples (so at most two), formula 3 asserts two distinct apples and that every apple is one of those two (exactly two), formula 2 forces any two apples to be identical (at most one), and formula 4 asserts a unique apple (exactly one).

The proposed mapping is: A → 3, B → 1, C → 2, D → 4. This is incorrect. C → 2 and D → 4 are correct, but A → 3 is wrong because A requires at most two apples while formula 3 asserts exactly two (stronger). B → 1 is wrong because B requires exactly two apples but formula 1 only forbids three distinct apples (it allows 0,1, or 2 apples), so it does not guarantee exactly two.

title: Which of the above statements are valid?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Practice Problems on Quantifiers and Predicate Logic
text: Which of the above statements are valid?
solution:
We interpret "valid" to mean that the implication is true in every structure with a non-empty domain.

We now analyse each of the four implications:

  1. ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃y ∀x P(x,y): This implication is not valid. It can be true that for every element x there is some element y (possibly depending on x) with P(x,y), while there is no single element y that works for all x. For example, let the domain be {1, 2} and let P(x,y) mean "x = y". For each x we can choose y = x, so the premise "for every x there exists a y with P(x,y)" is true. However, there is no single element that is equal to both 1 and 2, so there is no y such that P(x,y) holds for all x, and the conclusion fails in this structure.

  2. ∃x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∀y ∃x P(x,y): This implication is valid. If there is some element a such that P(a,y) holds for every y, then for each particular y we can simply choose that same element a as the witness. Thus, for every y there exists an x (namely, a) such that P(x,y) holds, so the conclusion is always true whenever the premise is true.

  3. ∀x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y): Assuming the domain is non-empty, this implication is valid. If P(x,y) holds for every pair (x,y), then in particular it holds for at least one concrete pair (a,b) from the domain. Therefore there exist x and y such that P(x,y), so the existential conclusion is guaranteed whenever the universal premise is true in a non-empty structure.

  4. ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y): Again assuming a non-empty domain, this implication is valid. If for every x there exists at least one y with P(x,y), then we can choose one particular element a from the domain and a corresponding element b such that P(a,b) holds. These a and b serve as witnesses for the existential statement "there exist x and y such that P(x,y)".

Therefore, the implications that are valid in every structure with a non-empty domain are: ∃x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∀y ∃x P(x,y), ∀x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y), and ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y).

optionFeedback.html: The implication "for every x there exists a y with P(x,y)" implies "there exists a single y that works for all x" is not valid. It can be true that each x has some y (possibly depending on x) with P(x,y), while no single y works for every x. For example, on the domain {1, 2} with P(x,y) meaning "x = y", the premise holds but there is no one element equal to both 1 and 2, so the conclusion fails.

The implication "there exists an x such that for all y, P(x,y)" implies "for every y there exists an x with P(x,y)" is valid. If there is some element a for which P(a,y) holds for every y, then for each specific y you can simply choose that same element a, so the condition "for every y there exists an x with P(x,y)" is automatically satisfied.

The implication "for all x and all y, P(x,y)" implies "there exist x and y such that P(x,y)" is valid as long as the domain is non-empty. If P holds for every pair (x,y), then in particular it holds for at least one specific pair, so the existential statement is always true in any non-empty structure.

The implication "for every x there exists a y with P(x,y)" implies "there exist x and y such that P(x,y)" is valid in any non-empty domain. If for each x there is at least one y with P(x,y), then in particular you can pick one concrete x and one corresponding y that satisfy P(x,y), giving witnesses for the existential statement.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q64
subject: Discrete Mathematics
subtopic: Practice Problems on Quantifiers and Predicate Logic
text:
Consider the following well-formed formula (WFF) of predicate logic:

∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) → (∃xP(x) → ∃xQ(x))

Which of the following statements about this WFF is correct?

options.html: Valid only if P(x) → Q(x) holds for every x in the domain

solution:
Concept

A predicate-logic formula is called valid — a logical validity, or a "tautology" of predicate logic — when it evaluates to true under every interpretation: every choice of a non-empty domain together with every assignment of meaning to the predicate symbols. One of the standard valid inference patterns is that from ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) and ∃xP(x), one can always derive ∃xQ(x), because the very element witnessing ∃xP(x) can be substituted into the universal conditional to also witness ∃xQ(x).

Application

  1. Take an arbitrary interpretation (any non-empty domain, with any meanings assigned to P and Q). If ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) is false in it, the whole formula is true automatically, since a false antecedent makes any implication true — so this case needs no further work.

  2. So assume ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) is true in this interpretation, and also assume the inner antecedent ∃xP(x) is true — pick a domain element a for which P(a) is true (existential instantiation).

  3. Apply ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) to this specific a (universal instantiation): P(a) → Q(a) is true.

  4. Since P(a) is true and P(a) → Q(a) is true, modus ponens gives Q(a) is true.

  5. Because Q(a) is true for this element a, ∃xQ(x) is true (existential generalization).

  6. So whenever ∃xP(x) is true, ∃xQ(x) is also true — the inner implication ∃xP(x) → ∃xQ(x) holds, and hence the whole formula holds in this arbitrary interpretation.

Cross-check

Try to falsify the formula instead: a conditional A → B is false only when A is true and B is false. Here that would need ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) true while ∃xP(x)→∃xQ(x) is false, i.e. ∃xP(x) true and ∃xQ(x) false. But ∃xP(x) true gives some element a with P(a) true; combined with ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) being true, this forces Q(a) true, which means ∃xQ(x) is true — contradicting ∃xQ(x) false. No interpretation can falsify the formula, and this argument never used the size of the domain, confirming the result holds for finite and infinite domains alike.

Since the formula evaluates to true under every interpretation, it is always valid — a tautology of predicate logic.

optionFeedback.html: In predicate logic, some claims genuinely depend on domain size — for example, the sentence ∃x∀y(x=y), asserting that every two elements of the domain are identical, is true in a domain containing a single member and false in every domain with more than one member, so its truth is a direct consequence of domain size.

In predicate logic, ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) is a contingent statement about a particular interpretation — its truth value changes depending on how P and Q are defined, so it can be true under one assignment of meanings to P and Q and false under another.

In predicate logic, formulas that are always valid — true in every interpretation without exception — are called logical validities or tautologies of predicate logic; a simple example is ∀x(P(x) → P(x)), which is true under every interpretation regardless of how P is defined, because nothing can fail to imply itself.

In predicate logic, logical equivalence requires identical truth values in every interpretation, not merely a related subject matter; for instance, 'it is raining and it is cold' is not logically equivalent to 'it is not sunny', since both statements can differ in truth value across many possible scenarios even though both concern the weather.
